title: Introduction to Quantum Mechanics
text:
Preface
Quantum mechanics is best learned through repeated reading and problem solving. Many concepts depend on one another, and ideas that seem unfamiliar at first often become clearer as you progress. These notes introduce many new concepts. If a term becomes unclear, use the search function to find where it was introduced. Sections marked with an asterisk (*) may be skipped without interrupting your progress through the remaining material.

title: Introduction to Quantum Mechanics
text:
Introduction
It is often said that quantum mechanics is a theory of the microscopic world. This is true in the sense that quantum effects are most easily observed in atoms, molecules, and other microscopic systems. However, it is not true in the sense that quantum mechanics applies only to microscopic systems. Quantum mechanics is a fundamental theory of nature and applies, in principle, to physical systems at every scale.
Why, then, are quantum effects easier to observe in atoms and other microscopic systems than in everyday objects? Part of the answer lies in how a system interacts with its surroundings. Microscopic systems can often be prepared and isolated well enough for their quantum behavior to remain observable. Everyday objects, by contrast, interact continually with air, light, and other parts of their environment.
These interactions do not cause quantum mechanics to stop applying. The object together with its environment still has a quantum state and evolves according to quantum mechanics. However, interaction causes the state of the object to become correlated with the state of the environment, so that the object can no longer generally be described independently of its surroundings. When we observe only the object and do not keep track of all the details of the environment, interference between different possible states of the object can rapidly become unobservable. This process is known as decoherence.
Decoherence is an important part of the transition from quantum to classical behavior, but it does not by itself produce classical mechanics. In macroscopic systems, characteristic actions are also typically much larger than \(\hbar\) so that quantum dynamics can approach classical dynamics under appropriate conditions. Classical mechanics is therefore not a rival theory that replaces quantum mechanics for large objects; rather, it is an effective theory that emerges from quantum mechanics in an appropriate limit.
Light provides an interesting contrast. Interference of light is easily observed on everyday scales and is accurately described by classical electromagnetic wave theory. However, classical interference is not a phenomenon separate from quantum interference. In the full quantum theory, light is a quantum electromagnetic field, and the familiar interference of classical optics emerges in the many-photon limit of the quantum theory. In this sense, ordinary optical interference is a macroscopic manifestation of quantum interference.
This connection becomes especially clear in single-photon experiments. Photons can be sent through an interferometer one at a time, yet after many detection events they build up the same interference pattern predicted by classical wave theory. Why can such interference remain observable over macroscopic distances? A major reason is that photons often interact only weakly with their surroundings. Even when light travels through air, passes through transparent glass, or reflects from a mirror, these interactions often do not strongly entangle the light with uncontrolled degrees of freedom in the environment. The environment therefore acquires little information about which path the light has taken, and the interference can survive. Photons also interact only very weakly with one another under ordinary conditions. As a result, the quantum interference of light can remain observable through many familiar optical processes. This is why the connection between the quantum description of light and classical wave optics is particularly direct.
The same principle applies more generally: a system need not be completely isolated for quantum behavior to remain observable. What matters is whether interactions with the environment strongly disturb the particular quantum behavior we are interested in. The internal states of atoms provide an important example. An atom may move through a gas and collide with other particles, yet its internal energy levels can remain sufficiently well defined that transitions between them appear as distinct lines in the atomic spectrum. Similarly, an atom’s spin can remain well defined through many collisions because such collisions often affect the atom’s motion much more strongly than its spin.
These examples show that interaction with the environment does not necessarily destroy all quantum behavior of a system. Different aspects of the same system can be affected very differently by the environment. Thus, the important distinction is not simply between microscopic and macroscopic systems. Whether quantum behavior remains observable depends not only on the size of the system, but also on what property of the system we are studying and how strongly that property is disturbed by its surroundings.

title: 1  Vectors and Quantum States
text:
1.1 The Stern–Gerlach experiment
We begin with a simple experiment and let its results guide us toward the principles of modern quantum mechanics. Our starting point is a spin-1/2 system: measuring its spin along any chosen direction gives only two possible outcomes. This two-state system provides a simple setting in which to explore quantum states and develop the vector-space language used to describe them.
Spin angular momentum \({\bf{S}}\) is an intrinsic property of a microscopic particle, just as charge and mass are. Charge and mass are scalars, whereas spin is a vector. Its magnitude is fixed, but its projection along a chosen spatial direction can take different, quantized values. For electrons, neutrons, and protons, there are just two possibilities: \(+ {\hbar/2}\) or \(- {\hbar/2}\). These are spin-1/2 particles. To avoid repeatedly writing \({\hbar/2}\), we define a new quantity \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\):
\[
{\bf{S}} \equiv \frac{\hbar }{2}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}
\tag{1.1}\]
Choose a direction in space defined by a unit vector \({\bf{n}}\). The quantity \({\sigma _n} \equiv {\boldsymbol{\sigma}} \cdot {\bf{n}}\) is the projection of \({\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\) along \({\bf{n}}\). When we measure \({\sigma _n}\) for a spin-1/2 particle, there are only two possible answers: \(+ 1\) or \(- 1\).
A Stern–Gerlach (SG) apparatus1 has a sensitive axis and measures the spin projection along that axis. With its axis oriented along \(x\), it acts as a \({\sigma _x}\) detector; with its axis along \(z\), it acts as a \({\sigma _z}\) detector. A spin-1/2 particle passing through the detector leaves through one of two exits, labelled \(+1\) and \(-1\), corresponding to the two possible values of \({\sigma _n}\).
Imagine a source continuously emitting spin-1/2 particles with random spin orientations. We make the beam weak enough that particles travel through the apparatus one at a time and do not interact with one another. We can now arrange the apparatuses as shown in Figure 1.1 and follow what happens to the particles.
Before reading the result of each experiment, pause and make a prediction. Keep track of what has been measured and which outgoing beam is allowed to continue.
Experiment 1: repeating a measurement. Place an SG detector immediately after the source, with its sensitive axis along \(z\), to measure \({\sigma _z}\). Particles from the random source leave through the \(+1\) and \(-1\) exits with equal probability. Block the \(-1\) exit to admit only particles with \({\sigma _z}=+1\), and place a second \({\sigma _z}\) detector in their path. This time the beam does not split: every particle leaves through the second detector’s \(+1\) exit.
Similarly, admitting only particles from the first detector’s \(-1\) exit makes every particle leave through the second detector’s \(-1\) exit. The same agreement holds whenever both detectors measure the same spin component and no intervening process changes the state. A repeated measurement gives the same result. Selecting an exit also gives us a way to prepare particles with a definite value of \({\sigma _n}\).
Experiment 2: reversing the detector. Turn the second detector around so that its sensitive axis points opposite to that of the first. Every particle admitted from the first detector’s \(+1\) exit now leaves through the second detector’s \(-1\) exit, and vice versa.2 Reversing the measurement axis reverses the sign of the result, as expected for a vector projection.
Experiment 3: measuring a different component. Use a \({\sigma _z}\) detector to admit only particles with \({\sigma _z}=+1\), then send them through a \({\sigma _x}\) detector. The beam splits evenly: \(50\%\) leave through the \(+1\) exit and \(50\%\) through the \(-1\) exit.
A natural classical interpretation is that the second detector has simply sorted the particles by another pre-existing property. If so, particles leaving its \(+1\) exit would have both \({\sigma _z}=+1\) and \({\sigma _x}=+1\), while those leaving its \(-1\) exit would have both \({\sigma _z}=+1\) and \({\sigma _x}=-1\).
Hold on to that prediction. The next experiment puts it to the test.
Experiment 4: testing the classical interpretation. Admit particles from the \({\sigma _x}=+1\) exit in Experiment 3 and send them through a third detector measuring \({\sigma _z}\). The classical interpretation predicts \({\sigma _z}=+1\) for every particle. Instead, the beam splits evenly: \(50\%\) give \({\sigma _z}=+1\) and \(50\%\) give \({\sigma _z}=-1\). Admitting particles from the \({\sigma _x}=-1\) exit gives the same result.
Compare this with Experiment 1. The only intervening change is the measurement of \({\sigma _x}\). After that measurement, the initially certain \({\sigma _z}=+1\) result is no longer certain. Measuring one spin component changes the predictions for another. In quantum mechanics, a spin state cannot have definite values of both \({\sigma _x}\) and \({\sigma _z}\).
Experiment 5: recombining the two paths. In Experiment 4, we admitted particles from just one exit of the \({\sigma _x}\) detector. Now introduce an ideal beam combiner between the second and third detectors, as shown in Figure 1.2. The combiner brings the two outgoing paths back together. No additional device records which path a particle takes.
If opening both paths merely combined the results of the two one-path cases, the final outcomes would still occur with equal probability. They do not. With both paths open and no record of which path a particle takes, every particle gives \(+1\) at the final detector. If a device records the path, an observer can determine the corresponding \(\sigma_x\) result, and the final detector again gives \(+1\) and \(-1\) with equal probability. The key distinction is whether the setup makes the path information available to an observer. The record need not actually be read. We will return to this distinction when we discuss measurement.
These experiments set the requirements for our theory: it must explain repeatable measurements, the effect of changing the measurement axis, and the difference between selecting one path and recombining both paths without recording the path.
Measurements along an arbitrary axis. Let the unit vectors \(\mathbf{n}\) and \(\mathbf{m}\) make an angle \(\theta\). Prepare particles with \(\sigma_n=+1\), then measure \(\sigma_m\). The probabilities of the two outcomes are
\[
P(\sigma_m=+1)=\cos^2(\theta/2),\qquad
P(\sigma_m=-1)=\sin^2(\theta/2).
\]
Experiments 1, 2, and 3 correspond to \(\theta=0\), \(\theta=\pi\), and \(\theta=\pi/2\), respectively. The mean result over many identically prepared particles is
\[
\langle\sigma_m\rangle
=(+1)\cos^2(\theta/2)+(-1)\sin^2(\theta/2)
=\cos\theta.
\]
Thus the mean follows the familiar rule for projecting a Cartesian vector, even though each individual measurement gives only \(+1\) or \(-1\).
Keep these experiments in mind as we turn to the mathematics. We will build the language of quantum mechanics step by step, then return to the puzzles that brought us here.

title: 1  Vectors and Quantum States
text:
1.2 Vector spaces
In classical mechanics, a system’s state is specified by the instantaneous values of its dynamical variables, such as the positions and momenta of its particles. Given the forces, an exact initial state determines the subsequent motion. This is classical determinism; statistical predictions arise when our knowledge of the initial state is incomplete.
A quantum state cannot be specified in the same way. Some observables, such as position and its corresponding momentum component, cannot simultaneously have definite values. Even a single electron cannot have definite spin projections along two nonparallel directions. We therefore distinguish the quantum state from the observables measured on the system. For an isolated system, the Schrödinger equation determines the state’s evolution, while the state generally predicts probabilities for measurement outcomes of the observables.
We will the vector-space formulation of quantum mechanics: pure states are represented by vectors, and observables by operators. Matrix mechanics and wave mechanics provide concrete representations of this framework. This chapter introduces the vectors; the next introduces the operators.
Quantum postulate for pure states. A pure quantum state contains all the information about a system at a given instant. It is represented by a nonzero vector in a complex vector space. We normally choose this vector to have unit norm. Multiplying a normalized state vector by an overall phase factor \(e^{i\alpha}\) does not change the physical state.
When you hear vector, you may picture an arrow in three-dimensional space. Keep that familiar picture, but make room for a second meaning: a vector can also represent a quantum state. We will call vectors in physical three-dimensional space Cartesian vectors and vectors representing quantum states state vectors. The latter belong to the system’s state space, or Hilbert space.
Dirac gave state vectors their own notation: \(\lvert\text{vector name}\rangle\). A vector written this way is called a ket. The symbols may look unfamiliar at first, but they obey the vector-space rules we are about to use.
For example, write \(|+z\rangle\) for the state prepared by admitting particles from the \(\sigma_z=+1\) exit of an SG detector, and \(|-z\rangle\) for the state prepared from its \(\sigma_z=-1\) exit. These kets belong to the spin state space; they are not arrows pointing along the spatial \(z\) axis.
Some useful vector-space identities are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Commutativity:}\quad &\lvert\psi_\alpha\rangle+\lvert\psi_\beta\rangle=\lvert\psi_\beta\rangle+\lvert\psi_\alpha\rangle\\
\text{Associativity:}\quad &(\lvert\psi_\alpha\rangle+\lvert\psi_\beta\rangle)+\lvert\psi_\gamma\rangle
=\lvert\psi_\alpha\rangle+(\lvert\psi_\beta\rangle+\lvert\psi_\gamma\rangle)\\
\text{Scalar multiplication:}\quad &c\lvert\psi\rangle=\lvert\psi\rangle c\\
\text{Scalar associativity:}\quad &c_1(c_2\lvert\psi\rangle)=(c_1c_2)\lvert\psi\rangle\\
\text{Scalar identity:}\quad &1\lvert\psi\rangle=\lvert\psi\rangle\\
\text{Distributivity:}\quad &(c_1+c_2)\lvert\psi\rangle=c_1\lvert\psi\rangle+c_2\lvert\psi\rangle\\
&c(\lvert\psi_\alpha\rangle+\lvert\psi_\beta\rangle)=c\lvert\psi_\alpha\rangle+c\lvert\psi_\beta\rangle
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.2}\]
Here \(c,{c_1},{c_2}\) are complex numbers. Read these identities as rules for working with vectors. A vector space is closed under addition and scalar multiplication: these operations always produce another vector in the same space.
Zero vector. Every vector space contains a zero vector, \(\left\vert  {{\rm{null}}} \right\rangle\), which may be thought of as having zero length. It is defined by the following condition for every vector \(|\psi\rangle\):
\[
\left\vert  {{\rm{null}}} \right\rangle + |\psi\rangle = |\psi\rangle , \qquad  \qquad  0|\psi\rangle = \left\vert  {{\rm{null}}} \right\rangle
\tag{1.3}\]
The zero vector is needed for vector addition and cancellation, but represents no physical state.
If \(|\psi_1\rangle\) and \(|\psi_2\rangle\) belong to the same vector space, their linear combination \(|\psi\rangle=c_1|\psi_1\rangle+c_2|\psi_2\rangle\) belongs to that space as well. A set of vectors is linearly dependent if some linear combination of them equals the zero vector with coefficients that are not all zero. In particular, the set \(\{|\psi\rangle,|\psi_1\rangle,|\psi_2\rangle\}\) is linearly dependent because \(|\psi\rangle-c_1|\psi_1\rangle-c_2|\psi_2\rangle=0\).

title: 1  Vectors and Quantum States
section: 1.3 Examples of complex linear vector spaces
text:
1.3 Examples of complex linear vector spaces
The word vector may bring an arrow to mind, but a vector space can contain other kinds of objects. What matters is how those objects add and how they multiply by scalars. In each example below, check that adding two members or multiplying a member by a complex number gives us another memeber within the collection.
Example 1: complex column vectors.
Let us start with some familiar object: a column of \(n\) complex numbers. Add two such columns element by element, or multiply every element by a complex number. The result is still a column with \(n\) components. These columns therefore form a complex vector space.
\[
\begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\\a_3\\\vdots\\a_n\end{pmatrix},\quad a_i\in\mathbb C;\qquad\lvert\mathrm{null}\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}
\tag{1.4}\]
Example 2: solutions of a homogeneous linear differential equation.
Now consider a different kind of object: a function that solves the equation
\[
\frac{{{d^2}}}{{d{t^2}}}x(t) + 2\beta \frac{d}{{dt}}x(t) + \omega _0^2x(t) = 0
\tag{1.5}\]
Here we allow complex-valued solutions. If \({x_1}(t)\) and \({x_2}(t)\) are solutions, any complex linear combination of them is also a solution. Thus, the collection of solutions forms a complex vector space.

title: 1  Vectors and Quantum States
text:
1.4 Bras and inner products
So far, we can add vectors and multiply them by complex numbers. To discuss their lengths and how they relate to one another, we need another operation. Think of the dot product of two Cartesian vectors: it takes two vectors and returns a number. An inner product generalizes this idea to complex vector spaces. It is a rule that assigns a complex number to each ordered pair of vectors.
Dirac introduced a neat notation for this operation. To write the inner product of \(|\varphi\rangle\) and \(|\psi\rangle\), we write the first vector as \(\langle\varphi|\), and place it next to the second vector’s ket. The two brackets fit together:
\[
\langle \varphi|  \cdot |\psi\rangle \equiv \langle \varphi|\psi\rangle = c
\tag{1.6}\] Here \(c\) is the resulting complex number. The inner product supplies the rule for calculating it; the bra–ket notation gives us a compact way to write it.
\(\langle\varphi|\) is called bra. A bra is the dual object associated with a ket. For now, we can work with this correspondence through the rules below. Kets and bras each form a complex vector space. The correspondence between them is antilinear: when we convert a ket into its corresponding bra, we take the complex conjugate of each coefficient. The conversion rules are
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\psi\rangle &\longleftrightarrow \langle\psi|,\\
c|\psi\rangle &\longleftrightarrow c^*\langle\psi|,\\
c_1|\alpha\rangle+c_2|\beta\rangle
&\longleftrightarrow c_1^*\langle\alpha|+c_2^*\langle\beta|.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.7}\]
We can now express the defining properties of the inner product in bra–ket notation.
Linearity in the ket and in the bra:
\[
\begin{array}{l} \langle \gamma\vert \left( {{c_1}\vert \alpha\rangle + {c_2}\vert \beta\rangle } \right) = {c_1}\langle \gamma|\alpha\rangle + {c_2}\langle \gamma|\beta\rangle ,\\ \left( {{c_1}\langle \gamma\vert {\rm{ + }}{c_2}\langle \beta\vert } \right)\vert \alpha\rangle = {c_1}\langle \gamma|\alpha\rangle + {c_2}\langle \beta|\alpha\rangle \end{array}
\tag{1.8}\]
Conjugate symmetry:
\[
\langle \varphi|\psi\rangle = \langle \psi|\varphi\rangle ^*
\tag{1.9}\]
Applying conjugate symmetry, Equation 1.9, to the inner product of a vector with itself. \[
\langle \psi|\psi\rangle = \langle \psi|\psi\rangle ^*
\tag{1.10}\] The result equals its own complex conjugate, so \(\langle \psi\|\psi\rangle\) must be real.
Positive definiteness. To make this quantity behave like a squared length, we require \[
\langle \psi|\psi\rangle \ge 0
\tag{1.11}\] Equality holds only for \(\vert \psi\rangle = \vert {{\rm{null}}}\rangle\).
A vector \(\vert \psi\rangle\) whose inner product with itself is one, \(\langle \psi\|\psi\rangle = 1\) is normalized. Any nonzero, unnormalized vector \(|\psi\rangle\) can be normalized as follows: \[
\left\vert  {\tilde \psi } \right\rangle = \frac{{|\psi\rangle }}{{\sqrt {\langle \psi|\psi\rangle } }}
\tag{1.12}\]
Let us put the bra–ket notation to work with column vectors. Here we can see every step of the calculation.
Example: inner products of column vectors. Complex column vectors form a complex vector space. Their standard inner product is obtained by multiplying the conjugate transpose of the first column by the second column. Thus, if a column represents a ket, its conjugate-transpose row represents the corresponding bra. For example,
\[
\begin{array}{l} |\phi\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{a_1}}\\ {{a_2}} \end{array}} \right) \leftrightarrow \langle \phi|  = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {a_1^*}&{a_2^*} \end{array}} \right)\\ |\psi\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{b_1}}\\ {{b_2}} \end{array}} \right) \leftrightarrow \langle \psi|  = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {b_1^*}&{b_2^*} \end{array}} \right) \end{array}
\tag{1.13}\] inner product \(\langle \phi|\psi\rangle\) can then be defined by ordinary matrix multiplication:
\[
\langle \phi|\psi\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {a_1^*}&{a_2^*} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{b_1}}\\ {{b_2}} \end{array}} \right) = a_1^*{b_1} + a_2^*{b_2}
\tag{1.14}\] definitions satisfy all the required properties. Check conjugate symmetry, Equation 1.9, explicitly by reversing the two vectors:
\[
\langle \psi|\phi\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {b_1^*}&{b_2^*} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{a_1}}\\ {{a_2}} \end{array}} \right) = b_1^*{a_1} + b_2^*{a_2} = {({b_1}a_1^* + {b_2}a_2^*)^*} = {\langle \phi|\psi\rangle ^*}
\tag{1.15}\]

title: 1  Vectors and Quantum States
text:
1.5 Orthogonality and basis vectors
Let us start with some familiar objects. Two Cartesian vectors \({\bf{a}},{\bf{b}}\) are perpendicular when \({\bf{a}} \cdot {\bf{b}} = 0\). At most three nonzero vectors in three-dimensional Cartesian space can be mutually perpendicular. Rotating such a set gives infinitely many alternative sets. But we can never find more than three mutually perpendicular vectors. That is why the dimension of Cartesian space is three.
Given mutually perpendicular unit vectors \({\bf{x}},{\bf{y}},{\bf{z}}\) in a Cartesian space, they are called basis vectors. Any Cartesian vector \({\bf{v}}\) can be expressed as the linear combination of basis vectors:
\[
{\bf{v}} = \left( {{\bf{x}} \cdot {\bf{v}}} \right){\bf{x}} + \left( {{\bf{y}} \cdot {\bf{v}}} \right){\bf{y}} + \left( {{\bf{z}} \cdot {\bf{v}}} \right){\bf{z}} = {v_x}{\bf{x}} + {v_y}{\bf{y}} + {v_z}{\bf{z}}
\tag{1.16}\] can collect the three components of \({\bf{v}}\) into a column vector:
\[
{\bf{v}} = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{v_x}}\\ {{v_y}}\\ {{v_z}} \end{array}} \right){\rm{ = }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\bf{x}} \cdot {\bf{v}}}\\ {{\bf{y}} \cdot {\bf{v}}}\\ {{\bf{z}} \cdot {\bf{v}}} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{1.17}\] a fixed vector \({\bf{v}}\) while you rotate the coordinate axes. Rotating the \({\bf{x}},{\bf{y}},{\bf{z}}\) axes changes the components of \({\bf{v}}\), even though the vector itself stays fixed.
In their own coordinate system, the Cartesian basis vectors always have the following column representations:
\[
{\bf{x}} = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1\\ 0\\ 0 \end{array}} \right), \qquad  {\bf{y}} = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0\\ 1\\ 0 \end{array}} \right), \qquad  {\bf{z}} = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0\\ 0\\ 1 \end{array}} \right)
\tag{1.18}\]
We can carry this familiar geometry into the complex vector space. Two nonzero vectors \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\) are orthogonal if and only if their inner product vanishes, \(\langle \psi\vert \phi\rangle = 0\). The dimension of a complex vector space is the maximum number of mutually orthogonal nonzero vectors. Using the inner product defined in Equation 1.14, we can find infinitely many orthogonal pairs of two-component columns. Here are three pairs of normalized vectors:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix};\\[0.6em]
&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix};\\[0.6em]
&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\i\end{pmatrix},\quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-i\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.19}\] any one of these pairs and we cannot find a third nonzero column vector orthogonal to both members. Thus, the vector space of two-component columns has dimension two.
A basis is a linearly independent set of vectors that spans the space; it need not be orthogonal or normalized. A set of \(N\) mutually orthogonal, normalized vectors in an \(N\)-dimensional vector space forms a complete orthonormal basis. Unless stated otherwise, the bases used in this book are complete and orthonormal. For any two vectors \(|i\rangle,|j\rangle\) in such a basis,
\[
\langle j|i\rangle = {\delta _{ij}}
\tag{1.20}\] symbol \({\delta _{ij}}\) is the Kronecker delta, defined by
\[
{\delta _{ij}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 1, & i = j\\ 0, & i \ne j \end{array} \right.
\tag{1.21}\]
Just like a Cartesian vector has a unique expansion in a Cartesian basis: every state vector has a unique expansion as a linear combination of the basis vectors. In an \(N\)-dimensional space with basis \(\{|i\rangle\}_{i=1}^{N}\), any vector \(|\psi\rangle\) can be written as
\[
|\psi\rangle = \sum\limits_i {{a_i}|i\rangle }
\tag{1.22}\] \({a_i}\) is the complex coefficient of \(|i\rangle\) in the expansion of \(|\psi\rangle\). To find a particular coefficient, lets say \(a_j\), apply the bra \(\langle j|\) to both sides. Orthogonality removes every term except the one we want:
\[
\langle j|\psi\rangle = \sum\limits_i {\langle j| {a_i}|i\rangle } = \sum\limits_i {{a_i}\langle j|i\rangle } = \sum\limits_i {{a_i}{\delta _{ij}}} = {a_j}
\tag{1.23}\] the component of \(|\psi\rangle\) along \(|j\rangle\) is \(\langle j|\psi\rangle\), and
\[
|\psi\rangle = \sum\limits_i {\langle i|\psi\rangle |i\rangle } = \sum\limits_i {|i\rangle } \langle i|\psi\rangle
\tag{1.24}\] identity reconstructs a vector from its components. In the final expression, moving the scalar \(\langle i|\psi\rangle\) to the right of the ket groups the factors as \(|i\rangle\langle i|\). The section on outer products, projection operators, and completeness explains the meaning of these factors.
Taking the corresponding bra, using Equation 1.7 and Equation 1.9, gives
\[
\langle \psi|  = \sum\limits_i {\langle \psi|i\rangle } \langle i|
\tag{1.25}\]

title: 1  Vectors and Quantum States
text:
1.6 Matrix representations of vectors
Once we have chosen an ordered orthonormal basis, we can gather the expansion coefficients in Equation 1.24 into a column. This gives a concrete representation of the state vector in the chosen basis:
\[
\lvert\psi\rangle:=\begin{pmatrix}\langle 1\vert\psi\rangle\\\langle 2\vert\psi\rangle\\\vdots\\\langle N\vert\psi\rangle\end{pmatrix}
\tag{1.26}\]
In this basis, each basis vector is represented as:
\[
|1\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1\\ 0\\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{array}} \right), \qquad  |2\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0\\ 1\\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{array}} \right), \qquad  \cdots \qquad  |N\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0\\ 0\\ \vdots \\ 1 \end{array}} \right)
\tag{1.27}\]
Always keep track of the basis attached to a column. Changing the basis changes the elements, so columns written in different bases must first be converted to a common basis before we combine them in a matrix calculation.
The comparison below connects state-vector notation to Cartesian geometry. Here \(\mathbf{e}_i\) denotes a Cartesian basis vector. In both settings, an orthonormal basis lets us obtain a vector’s components by taking inner products with the basis vectors:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Cartesian vectors} & \text{Complex state vectors}\\[0.5em]
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{a}
& \langle\phi|\psi\rangle=\langle\psi|\phi\rangle^*\\[0.5em]
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0
& \langle\phi|\psi\rangle=0\\[0.5em]
\text{Orthonormal Cartesian basis}
& \text{Orthonormal basis }\{|i\rangle\}\\[0.5em]
v_i=\mathbf{e}_i\cdot\mathbf{v}
& a_i=\langle i|\psi\rangle\\[0.5em]
\mathbf{v}=\sum_i v_i\mathbf{e}_i
& |\psi\rangle=\sum_i a_i|i\rangle
\end{array}
\tag{1.28}\]

title: 1  Vectors and Quantum States
text:
1.7 Exercises
1.1 Given
\[
|\chi\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}2\\i\end{pmatrix} \quad \rm{ and }\quad |\eta\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
\]write their bras, calculate \(\langle\chi|\eta\rangle\) and \(\langle\eta|\chi\rangle\), and normalize \(|\chi\rangle\). Check conjugate symmetry.
1.2. Test each collection below: does it form a complex vector space under the usual addition and scalar multiplication? Focus on the vector-space rules; an inner product and completeness are not required.

All complex numbers.
All vectors in three-dimensional Cartesian space.
All complex-valued solutions \(\psi(x)\) of the following equation on a fixed interval, with fixed real \(E\) and a finite, continuous \(V(x)\). No normalization or boundary conditions are imposed.

\[
\left[ { - \frac{{{\hbar ^2}}}{{2m}}\frac{{{d^2}}}{{d{x^2}}} + V(x)} \right]\psi (x) = E\psi (x)
\tag{1.29}\]
1.3. Prove the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, \(\langle \alpha|\alpha\rangle \langle \beta|\beta\rangle \ge {\left\vert  {\langle \alpha|\beta\rangle } \right\vert ^2}\).
Hint: construct \(\vert \psi \rangle\) as a suitable linear combination of \(\vert \alpha\rangle\) and \(\vert \beta\rangle\), and use the nonnegative squared norm in Equation 1.11.
1.4. A vector \(|\psi\rangle\) in a two-dimensional complex vector space has the following expansion in the orthonormal basis \(\left\{ {\vert {\alpha _1}\rangle ,\vert {\alpha _2}\rangle } \right\}\):
\[
\vert \psi \rangle = \vert {\alpha _1}\rangle + 3\vert {\alpha _2}\rangle
\tag{1.30}\]
A second basis \(\left\{ {\vert {\beta _1}\rangle ,\vert {\beta _2}\rangle } \right\}\) satisfies
\[
\left\vert  {{\beta _1}} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\vert {\alpha _1}\rangle + i\vert {\alpha _2}\rangle } \right), \qquad  \left\vert  {{\beta _2}} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\vert {\alpha _1}\rangle - i\vert {\alpha _2}\rangle } \right)
\tag{1.31}\] \(|\psi\rangle\) in the second basis using two different methods, and check that your answers agree.

title: 1  Vectors and Quantum States
text:
A Stern–Gerlach apparatus separates particles through the interaction of their magnetic moment with a nonuniform magnetic field. For the systems considered here, the magnetic moment is proportional to the spin, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}=\gamma\mathbf{S}\), where \(\gamma\) is a constant. The exits can therefore be labelled by the measured spin projection.↩︎
Keep the laboratory \(z\) axis fixed. A detector pointing along \(+z\) measures \(\sigma_z\), whereas one pointing along \(-z\) measures \(\sigma_{-z}=-\sigma_z\). The sign change refers to the projection assigned by the detector; rotating the detector does not itself reverse the incoming particle’s spin. We do not need the details of the particle’s trajectory inside the apparatus to interpret the two readings.↩︎

title: 2  Operators
text:
2.1 Linear operators
A quantum state tells us about a system; an observable describes something we can measure, such as its position, momentum, or angular momentum. In the previous chapter, we represented states by vectors in a complex vector space. We now introduce the objects that act on those vectors: linear operators. They not only transform quantum states but also provide the mathematical object for observables.
Think of an operator as a machine: put in a vector, and another vector comes out. We usually place a hat over its symbol to distinguish it from a number variable. If the operator \(\hat O\) takes the input vector \(|\psi\rangle\) to the output vector \(|\phi\rangle\), we write
\[
\hat O\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \left\vert  \phi \right\rangle
\tag{2.1}\] operator can also act on a bra, producing another bra:
\[
\left\langle \alpha \right\vert \hat O = \left\langle \beta \right\vert
\tag{2.2}\] operator acting on a ket is written to its left; an operator acting on a bra is written to its right. An operator between a bra and a ket obeys associativity:
\[
\langle \alpha \vert \left( {\hat O\vert \beta\rangle } \right) \equiv \left( {\langle \alpha \vert \hat O} \right)\vert \beta\rangle \equiv \langle \alpha \vert \hat O\vert \beta\rangle
\tag{2.3}\] result is a complex number. You can read the expression in two steps: first let \(\hat O\) act on \(|\beta\rangle\), then take the inner product of the resulting vector with \(|\alpha\rangle\). The parentheses change how we group the calculation, but not its answer.
Let us first learn the basic rules of operators.
Equality. Two operators are equal if they give the same output for every input vector: if \(\hat X|\psi\rangle=\hat Y|\psi\rangle\) for every \(|\psi\rangle\), then \(\hat X=\hat Y\).
Identity. The identity operator \(\hat I\) is the machine that does nothing: every input comes out unchanged.
\[
\hat I\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \left\vert  \psi \right\rangle
\tag{2.4}\]
Products. An operator product describes a sequence of operations. In \(\hat X\hat Y|\psi\rangle\), the operator closest to the ket acts first: apply \(\hat Y\), then \(\hat X\). Thus \(\hat X\hat Y\) is itself an operator.
\[
\left( {\hat X\hat Y} \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \equiv \hat X\left( {\hat Y\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle } \right) = \hat X\hat Y\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle
\tag{2.5}\]
\[
\left\langle \psi \right\vert \left( {\hat X\hat Y} \right) \equiv \left( {\left\langle \psi \right\vert \hat X} \right)\hat Y = \left\langle \psi \right\vert \hat X\hat Y
\tag{2.6}\]
The order generally matters: \(\hat X\hat Y\ne\hat Y\hat X\). For a familiar analogy, imagine rotating a book by \(90^\circ\) about one axis and then about a different axis. Reversing those rotations can leave the book facing a different direction. Operator products have the same sensitivity to order.
Powers of an operator are defined by
\[
{\hat X^n} \equiv \underbrace {\hat X\hat X \cdots \hat X}_{n\text{ terms}}
\tag{2.7}\] multiplication is associative: grouping the operations differently does not change their order or their result.
\[
\hat X\left( {\hat Y\hat Z} \right) = \left( {\hat X\hat Y} \right)\hat Z = \hat X\hat Y\hat Z
\tag{2.8}\] any operator by the identity leaves it unchanged:
\[
\hat I\hat X = \hat X\hat I = \hat X
\tag{2.9}\]
What makes an operator linear? It acts on each term of a superposition separately, and numerical coefficients pass through unchanged. In particular, \(\hat X(c_\alpha|\psi_\alpha\rangle+c_\beta|\psi_\beta\rangle)=c_\alpha\hat X|\psi_\alpha\rangle+c_\beta\hat X|\psi_\beta\rangle\). The first two rules below express linearity; the remaining rules describe operator addition.
\[
\begin{gathered} \hat X\left( {c\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle } \right) = c\hat X\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle , \\ \hat X\left( {\left\vert  {{\psi _\alpha }} \right\rangle + \left\vert  {{\psi _\beta }} \right\rangle } \right) = \hat X\left\vert  {{\psi _\alpha }} \right\rangle + \hat X\left\vert  {{\psi _\beta }} \right\rangle , \\ \left( {\hat X + \hat Y} \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \hat X\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle + \hat Y\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \\ \hat X + \hat Y = \hat Y + \hat X, \\ \hat X + (\hat Y + \hat Z) = (\hat X + \hat Y) + \hat Z \\ \end{gathered}
\tag{2.10}\]
The third property in Equation eq-zeqnnum324323, together with the properties of the inner product, gives
\[
\left\langle \alpha \right\vert \left( {{\hat X + \hat Y}} \right)\left\vert  \beta \right\rangle = \left\langle \alpha \right\vert \hat X\left\vert  \beta \right\rangle + \left\langle \alpha \right\vert \hat Y\left\vert  \beta \right\rangle
\tag{2.11}\]

title: 2  Operators
text:
2.2 Matrix representations of operators
A basis allows us to represent an abstract vector by a column of numbers, as in Equation eq-zeqnnum935342. It also allows us to represent an operator by a matrix. Let \(\{|1\rangle,|2\rangle,\ldots,|N\rangle\}\) be an orthonormal basis, and suppose
\[
\hat M\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \left\vert  \phi \right\rangle
\tag{2.12}\]
Multiply both sides from the left by \(\langle i|\), we have both sides equal to the \(i\) th component of \(|\phi\rangle\)
\[
\left\langle i \right\vert \hat M\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \left\langle {i} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {i \phi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\phi } \right\rangle
\tag{2.13}\]
Using \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \sum {\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle {j} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {j \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle }\), we can rewrite Equation eq-zeqnnum456036 as
\[
\sum\limits_{j = 1}^N {\left\langle i \right\vert \hat M\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle {j} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {j \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } = \left\langle {i} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {i \phi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\phi } \right\rangle
\tag{2.14}\]
The quantity \(\left\langle i \right\vert \hat M\left\vert  j \right\rangle\) is a number. Write \({M_{ij}} \equiv \left\langle i \right\vert \hat M\left\vert  j \right\rangle\) and let \(i\) in Equation eq-zeqnnum775889 run through the entire basis to obtain
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{M_{11}}}&{{M_{12}}}& \cdots &{{M_{1N}}}\\ {{M_{21}}}&{{M_{22}}}& \cdots &{{M_{2N}}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ {{M_{N1}}}&{{M_{N2}}}& \cdots &{{M_{NN}}} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\langle 1\vert \psi\rangle }\\ {\langle 2\vert \psi\rangle }\\ \vdots \\ {\langle N\vert \psi\rangle } \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\langle 1\vert \phi \rangle }\\ {\langle 2\vert \phi \rangle }\\ \vdots \\ {\langle N\vert \phi \rangle } \end{array}} \right)
\tag{2.15}\]
This is ordinary matrix multiplication: a matrix acts on the column vector and produces another column vector. It represents \(\hat M|\psi\rangle=|\phi\rangle\) in the chosen basis.
Thus, the matrix representation of \(\hat M\) in the chosen basis is
\[
\hat M = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{M_{11}}}&{{M_{12}}}& \cdots &{{M_{1N}}}\\ {{M_{21}}}&{{M_{22}}}& \cdots &{{M_{2N}}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ {{M_{N1}}}&{{M_{N2}}}& \cdots &{{M_{NN}}} \end{array}} \right), \qquad  {M_{ij}} \equiv \left\langle i \right\vert \hat M\left\vert  j \right\rangle
\tag{2.16}\]
A useful way to read the matrix is one column at a time. Column \(j\) lists the components of \(\hat M|j\rangle\). Like a state vector’s column representation, an operator’s matrix depends on the chosen basis.

title: 2  Operators
text:
2.3 Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Most vectors change their direction in vector space when an operator acts on them. An eigenvector of the operator is special: the output is simply a number times the input. That number is the eigenvalue corresponding to the eigenvector. In a real vector space, picture an arrow that is stretched, shortened, or reversed without leaving its original line. In a complex vector space, the eigenvalue can be a complex number. An eigenvector must be nonzero. We often label it by its eigenvalue: \(|a_i\rangle\) denotes an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(a_i\).
Example. If \(\hat A\) has eigenvectors \(\vert {a_i}\rangle\) with eigenvalues \({a_i}\), then
\[
\hat A\left\vert  {{a_1}} \right\rangle = {a_1}\left\vert  {{a_1}} \right\rangle ,\;\; \qquad  \hat A\left\vert  {{a_2}} \right\rangle = {a_2}\left\vert  {{a_2}} \right\rangle , \qquad  \cdots
\tag{2.17}\]
When operators are represented by square matrices and vectors by columns, these are precisely the matrix eigenvalues and eigenvectors of linear algebra. We can therefore find an operator’s eigenvalues and eigenvectors from its matrix representation.
Several linearly independent eigenvectors can share the same eigenvalue. The number of independent eigenvectors sharing that value is its degeneracy. A degeneracy of one means the eigenvalue is nondegenerate.
Theorem 2.1. If several eigenvectors of \(\hat A\) share an eigenvalue, any nonzero linear combination of them is an eigenvector with that same eigenvalue.
Proof. Suppose eigenvalue \(a\) of \(\hat A\) has \(n\) eigenvectors, denoted \(\vert 1\rangle ,\vert 2\rangle , \cdots \vert n\rangle\), so that
\[
\hat A\left\vert  i \right\rangle = a\left\vert  i \right\rangle , \qquad  i = 1,2, \cdots n
\tag{2.18}\]
For any linear combination \(\sum\nolimits_i {{c_i}\vert i\rangle }\) of these eigenvectors,
\[
\hat A\left( {\sum\limits_i {{c_i}\vert i\rangle } } \right) = \sum\limits_i {{c_i}\hat A\vert i\rangle } = \sum\limits_i {{c_i}a\vert i\rangle } = a\left( {\sum\limits_i {{c_i}\vert i\rangle } } \right)
\tag{2.19}\] proves the result: within a subspace whose vectors all share eigenvalue \(a\), the operator simply multiplies every vector by \(a\).

title: 2  Operators
section: 2.4 Outer products, projection operators, and completeness
text:
2.4 Outer products, projection operators, and completeness
In Dirac notation, a combination of symbols is legal if it yields a valid object in vector space, which are a number, a ket , a bra or an operator. For example, \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\) produces a number, an operator acting on a ket produces a ket, and an operator acting on a bra produces a bra. On the other hand, \(\langle\phi|+|\psi\rangle\) is illegal, \(\hat X\langle\psi|\) and \(|\psi\rangle\hat X\) are also illegal. But what kind of object is this \[
\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \left\langle \phi \right\vert
\] {#eq-zeqnnum460948}This is an outer product. It is an operator. Why?
Dirac notation has a useful associative rule: in a product of kets, bras, numbers, and operators, brackets \(\left( {} \right)\) may group adjacent factors in any way, provided the expression inside \(\left( {} \right)\) is a valid object.
To interpret the outer product in Equation eq-zeqnnum460948, multiply it on the right by a ket and use associativity:
\[
\left( {\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \left\langle \phi \right\vert } \right)\;\left\vert  \alpha \right\rangle = \left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \;\left( {\left\langle {\phi } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\phi \alpha }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\alpha } \right\rangle } \right)
\tag{2.20}\]
The right-hand side is the number \(\left\langle {\phi } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\phi \alpha }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\alpha } \right\rangle\) times the ket \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\), so it is another ket. An outer product therefore maps a ket to a ket: it is an operator.

2.4.1 Projection operators
Let \(\{|j\rangle\}\) be a complete orthonormal basis. We can split any vector \(|\psi\rangle\) into components along the basis directions. Associativity lets us rewrite that expansion as
\[
\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \sum\limits_j {\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle {j} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {j \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } = \sum\limits_j {\left( {\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle }
\] {#eq-zeqnnum153427}Every term in this sum contains an outer-product operator.
\[
\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert \equiv {\hat P}_j
\] {#eq-ch02-p0320}This is a projection operator. Think of a Cartesian vector’s projection on a coordinate axis: the projector \(|j\rangle\langle j|\) keeps the component along \(|j\rangle\) and discards all components orthogonal to it.
\[
\left( {\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle {j} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {j \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle
\] {#eq-ch02-p0322}Projecting twice changes nothing further: once only the \(|j\rangle\) component remains, the same projector leaves it alone. Thus \(\hat P_j^2=\hat P_j\).


2.4.2 The completeness relation
In Equation eq-zeqnnum153427, \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) does not depend on the summation index \(j\) and can be taken outside the sum:
\[
\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \left( {\sum\limits_j {\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } } \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle
\tag{2.21}\]
Since \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) is arbitrary, the summation of the projectors must be the identity operator:
\[
\sum\limits_j {\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } = \hat I
\tag{2.22}\]
This is the completeness relation: splitting a vector into all its basis components and reassembling them recovers the original vector. We can insert this form of the identity anywhere an operator is allowed, without changing the expression. This is a very useful method.
For example, inserting it on both sides of \(\hat M\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c} \hat M = \left( {\sum\limits_i {\left\vert  i \right\rangle \left\langle i \right\vert } } \right)\hat M\left( {\sum\limits_j {\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } } \right) = \sum\limits_{i,j} {\left\vert  i \right\rangle \left\langle i \right\vert \hat M\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } \\ = \sum\limits_{i,j} {\left\langle i \right\vert \hat M\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\vert  i \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } = \sum\limits_{i,j} {{M_{ij}}\left\vert  i \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } \end{array}
\] {#eq-ch02-p0329}If the orthonormal basis consists of eigenvectors satisfying \(\hat M|j\rangle=m_j|j\rangle\), the expression simplifies. Each projector selects one component, and the corresponding eigenvalue tells us how much \(\hat M\) multiplies that component:
\[
\begin{array}{c} \hat M = \sum\limits_{i,j} {\left\langle i \right\vert \hat M\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\vert  i \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } = \sum\limits_{i,j} {{m_j}\langle i\vert j\rangle \left\vert  i \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } = \sum\limits_{i,j} {{m_j}{\delta _{ij}}\left\vert  i \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } \\ = \sum\limits_j {{m_j}\left\vert  j \right\rangle \left\langle j \right\vert } \end{array}
\tag{2.23}\]

title: 2  Operators
text:
2.5 Hermitian conjugates of operators
The dual of a ket is a bra. If \(\hat A|\psi\rangle=|\phi\rangle\), the corresponding bra relation is \(\langle\psi|\hat A^{\dagger}=\langle\phi|\). The operator \(\hat A^{\dagger}\) is the Hermitian conjugate, or adjoint, of \(\hat A\). Read the superscript \(\dagger\) as “dagger.” This relation must hold for every input ket.
\[
\hat A \leftrightarrow {\hat A^\dagger }
\tag{2.24}\]
Hermitian conjugate obeys the following theorems \[
(c\hat A)^{\dagger}=c^*\hat A^{\dagger}
\].
Theorem 2.2. The adjoint of a sum is the sum of the adjoints.
\[
{\left( {\hat X + \hat Y} \right)^\dagger } = {\hat X^\dagger } + {\hat Y^\dagger }
\tag{2.25}\]
Proof. Apply the bra–ket duality rules Equation eq-zeqnnum136783 and Equation eq-zeqnnum326007:
\[
\begin{array}{c} \left( {\hat X + \hat Y} \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \leftrightarrow \left\langle \psi \right\vert {\left( {\hat X + \hat Y} \right)^\dagger }\\ \left( {\hat X + \hat Y} \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \hat X\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle + \hat Y\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \leftrightarrow \left\langle \psi \right\vert {{\hat X}^\dagger } + \left\langle \psi \right\vert {{\hat Y}^\dagger } = \left\langle \psi \right\vert ({{\hat X}^\dagger } + {{\hat Y}^\dagger }) \end{array}
\tag{2.26}\]
Theorem 2.3. Taking the adjoint of a product reverses the order of its factors.
\[
{\left( {\hat X\hat Y} \right)^\dagger } = {\hat Y^\dagger }{\hat X^\dagger }
\tag{2.27}\]
Proof.
\[
\begin{array}{c} \left( {\hat X\hat Y} \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \leftrightarrow \left\langle \psi \right\vert {\left( {\hat X\hat Y} \right)^\dagger }\\ \left( {\hat X\hat Y} \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \hat X\left( {\hat Y\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle } \right) \leftrightarrow \left( {\left\langle \psi \right\vert {{\hat Y}^\dagger }} \right){{\hat X}^\dagger } = \left\langle \psi \right\vert {{\hat Y}^\dagger }{{\hat X}^\dagger } \end{array}
\tag{2.28}\]
Theorem 2.4. Taking the adjoint exchanges the two states in a matrix element and complex-conjugates the resulting number.
For any two vectors \(\vert \alpha\rangle ,\vert \beta\rangle\),
\[
\langle\alpha|\hat M^{\dagger}|\beta\rangle=\bigl(\langle\beta|\hat M|\alpha\rangle\bigr)^*
\tag{2.29}\]
Proof. Put \(\hat M\left\vert  \alpha \right\rangle = \left\vert  \gamma \right\rangle\), so that \(\left\langle \alpha \right\vert {\hat M^\dagger } = \left\langle \gamma \right\vert\).
\[
\langle\alpha|\hat M^{\dagger}|\beta\rangle=\langle\gamma|\beta\rangle=\bigl(\langle\beta|\gamma\rangle\bigr)^*=\bigl(\langle\beta|\hat M|\alpha\rangle\bigr)^*
\tag{2.30}\]
Theorem 2.5. Taking the adjoint twice returns the original operator.
\[
{({\hat M^\dagger })^\dagger } = \hat M
\tag{2.31}\]
Proof. For any two vectors \(\vert \alpha\rangle ,\vert \beta\rangle\),
\[
\langle\alpha|(\hat M^{\dagger})^{\dagger}|\beta\rangle=\bigl(\langle\beta|\hat M^{\dagger}|\alpha\rangle\bigr)^*=\Bigl[\bigl(\langle\alpha|\hat M|\beta\rangle\bigr)^*\Bigr]^*=\langle\alpha|\hat M|\beta\rangle
\tag{2.32}\]
The first two equalities use Theorem 2.4. Hence \({({\hat M^\dagger })^\dagger } = \hat M\).

2.5.1 Hermitian conjugation of an outer product
For an outer-product operator \(\vert \psi \rangle \langle \phi \vert\),
\[
\left( {\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \left\langle \phi \right\vert } \right)\left\vert  \alpha \right\rangle {\rm{ = }}\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \left\langle {\phi } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\phi \alpha }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\alpha } \right\rangle \leftrightarrow \left\langle {\alpha } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\alpha \phi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\phi } \right\rangle \left\langle \psi \right\vert {\rm{ = }}\left\langle \alpha \right\vert \left( {\left\vert  \phi \right\rangle \left\langle \psi \right\vert } \right)
\tag{2.33}\]
Therefore its Hermitian conjugate is
\[
{\left( {\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle \left\langle \phi \right\vert } \right)^\dagger } = \left\vert  \phi \right\rangle \left\langle \psi \right\vert
\tag{2.34}\]


2.5.2 Matrix representation of the Hermitian conjugate
In a basis \(\left\{ {\left\vert  1 \right\rangle ,\left\vert  2 \right\rangle ...\left\vert  N \right\rangle } \right\}\), Equation eq-zeqnnum961324 relates the matrix elements of \(\hat M\) and \({\hat M^\dagger }\) as follows:
\[
\langle i|\hat M^{\dagger}|j\rangle=\bigl(\langle j|\hat M|i\rangle\bigr)^*\qquad\text{or}\qquad (M^{\dagger})_{ij}=M_{ji}^*
\tag{2.35}\]
For matrices, taking the adjoint is a two-step recipe: transpose the matrix (exchange rows and columns), then complex-conjugate every element. For example,
\[
\text{If } \hat M = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{M_{11}}}&{{M_{12}}}&{{M_{13}}} \\ {{M_{21}}}&{{M_{22}}}&{{M_{23}}} \\ {{M_{31}}}&{{M_{32}}}&{{M_{33}}} \end{array}} \right), \qquad  \;\;\;\;\text{then } {\hat M^\dagger } = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {M_{11}^*}&{M_{21}^*}&{M_{31}^*} \\ {M_{12}^*}&{M_{22}^*}&{M_{32}^*} \\ {M_{13}^*}&{M_{23}^*}&{M_{33}^*} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{2.36}\]
The matrix representation makes it clear that \({\left( {{{\hat M}^\dagger }} \right)^\dagger } = \hat M\). Thus \(\hat M\) and \({\hat M^\dagger }\) are Hermitian conjugates of one another.

title: 2  Operators
text:
2.6 Inverse and unitary operators
Inverse. An inverse operator undoes the action of another operator. If \(\hat O\) takes an input to an output, \(\hat O^{-1}\) takes that output back to the input. Not every operator has an inverse: a projector onto a proper subspace, for instance, discards components that cannot be recovered. When the inverse exists, it satisfies
\[
{\hat O^{ - 1}}\hat O = \hat O{\hat O^{ - 1}} = \hat I
\tag{2.37}\]
Unitary operator. An operator \(\hat U\) is unitary when its adjoint is also its inverse: \(\hat U^{\dagger}=\hat U^{-1}\), or equivalently \(\hat U^{\dagger}\hat U=\hat U\hat U^{\dagger}=\hat I\). Its action is called a unitary transformation. Think of a rotation that preserves lengths and angles; a unitary transformation is the complex-vector-space counterpart. It preserves inner products.
Theorem 2.6. A unitary transformation preserves inner products.
Proof. Suppose \(\hat U\left\vert  \alpha \right\rangle = \left\vert  {\alpha '} \right\rangle\) and \(\hat U\left\vert  \beta \right\rangle = \left\vert  {\beta '} \right\rangle\). Then
\[
\left\langle {{\alpha '}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{\alpha '} {\beta '}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\beta '}} \right\rangle = \left\langle \alpha \right\vert {\hat U^\dagger }\hat U\left\vert  \beta \right\rangle = \left\langle {\alpha } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\alpha \beta }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\beta } \right\rangle
\tag{2.38}\]
Setting the two input vectors equal in Theorem 2.6 shows that unitary transformations also preserve norms.

title: 2  Operators
text:
2.7 Hermitian operators
An operator \(\hat A\) is Hermitian if it equals its own adjoint: \(\hat A^{\dagger}=\hat A\). Hermitian operators are central to quantum mechanics because they represent observables. The results below explain why: their eigenvalues are real, and their eigenvectors can form an orthonormal basis.
For a Hermitian operator, exchanging the two states in a matrix element gives its complex conjugate. Using the adjoint relation from Theorem 2.4, we obtain
\[
\langle\phi|\hat X|\psi\rangle=\bigl(\langle\psi|\hat X|\phi\rangle\bigr)^*
\tag{2.39}\]
Theorem 2.7. For a Hermitian operator \(\hat X\), \(\left\langle \psi \right\vert \hat X\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) is real.
Proof. Set \(\left\vert  \phi \right\rangle = \left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) in Equation eq-zeqnnum353712:
\[
\langle\psi|\hat X|\psi\rangle=\bigl(\langle\psi|\hat X|\psi\rangle\bigr)^*
\tag{2.40}\]
Theorem 2.8. The eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator are real.
Proof. If \(\hat A\left\vert  a \right\rangle = a\left\vert  a \right\rangle\), duality gives \(\left\langle a \right\vert {\hat A^\dagger } = \left\langle a \right\vert {a^*}\) and \(\hat A = {\hat A^\dagger }\), hence \(\left\langle a \right\vert \hat A = \left\langle a \right\vert {a^*}\). We can therefore evaluate \(\left\langle a \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  a \right\rangle\) in two ways:
\[
\begin{array}{c} \left\langle a \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  a \right\rangle = \left\langle a \right\vert \left( {\hat A\left\vert  a \right\rangle } \right) = a\left\langle {a} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {a a}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {a} \right\rangle \\ \left\langle a \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  a \right\rangle = \left( {\left\langle a \right\vert \hat A} \right)\left\vert  a \right\rangle = {a^*}\left\langle {a} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {a a}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {a} \right\rangle \end{array}
\tag{2.41}\]
Since an eigenvector is nonzero, \(\langle a|a\rangle>0\). Dividing both expressions by this squared norm gives \(a=a^*\), so \(a\) is real.
Physically, this ensures that measured values of observables are real.
Theorem 2.9. A Hermitian operator’s matrix equals its conjugate transpose, and its diagonal elements are real.
Proof. By Equation eq-zeqnnum961324, if \(\hat A\) is Hermitian, then for any vectors \(\vert \alpha\rangle ,\vert \beta\rangle\),
\[
\langle\alpha|\hat A|\beta\rangle=\bigl(\langle\beta|\hat A|\alpha\rangle\bigr)^*
\tag{2.42}\]
Consequently, the matrix elements of \(\hat A\) in any complete basis obey
\[
{A_{ij}} = A_{ji}^*
\tag{2.43}\]
On the diagonal, this becomes \(A_{ii}=A_{ii}^*\), so every diagonal element is real. Off the diagonal, elements occur in complex-conjugate pairs across the main diagonal.
This gives a quick visual check: the diagonal elements must be real, and each element above the diagonal must be the complex conjugate of its partner below it.
Theorem 2.10. Eigenvectors of a Hermitian operator belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.
Proof. Let \({a_i}\) and \({a_j}\) be eigenvalues of the Hermitian operator \(\hat A\), with corresponding eigenvectors \(\vert {a_i}\rangle ,\vert {a_j}\rangle\):
\[
\begin{array}{c} \hat A\left\vert  {{a_i}} \right\rangle = {a_i}\left\vert  {{a_i}} \right\rangle \\ \hat A\left\vert  {{a_j}} \right\rangle = {a_j}\left\vert  {{a_j}} \right\rangle \end{array}
\tag{2.44}\]
Duality gives
\[
\left\langle {{a_i}} \right\vert {\hat A^\dagger } = \left\langle {{a_i}} \right\vert a_i^*
\tag{2.45}\]
Since \(\hat A = {\hat A^\dagger }\) and Hermitian eigenvalues are real, this becomes
\[
\left\langle {{a_i}} \right\vert \hat A = \left\langle {{a_i}} \right\vert {a_i}
\tag{2.46}\]
Multiply both sides on the right by \(\vert {a_j}\rangle\), then let \(\hat A\) act first on \(\vert {a_j}\rangle\). Rearranging gives
\[
\left( {{a_j} - {a_i}} \right)\left\langle {{{a_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_i}} {{a_j}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{a_j}}} \right\rangle = 0
\tag{2.47}\]
Since \({a_i} \ne {a_j}\), we must have \(\langle {{a_i}}\vert {{a_j}}\rangle = 0\), proving the result.
In an \(N\)-dimensional space, \(N\) mutually orthogonal nonzero vectors provide all the basis directions we need. Therefore,
Theorem 2.11. If all \(N\) eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator \(\hat A\) are nondegenerate, its \(N\) mutually orthogonal eigenvectors \(\{ \vert {a_1}\rangle ,\vert {a_2}\rangle \cdots \vert {a_N}\rangle \}\) form a complete basis for the vector space. After normalization, they form an orthonormal basis.
The conclusion extends to degenerate Hermitian operators. Chapter 4 discusses how to choose the basis vectors within degenerate subspaces.

2.7.1 Representations
Choosing a representation means choosing the basis in which we write vector space objects. A complete orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of \(\hat A\) defines the \(\hat A\) representation. In this basis, \(\hat A\) acts particularly simply: it multiplies each component by its eigenvalue, without mixing components.

An arbitrary vector \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) has the following column of components in the \(\hat A\) representation:

\[
\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \sum\limits_i {\left\vert  {{a_i}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{a_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_i}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\left\langle {{{a_1}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_1}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle }\\ {\left\langle {{{a_2}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_2}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle }\\ \vdots \end{array}} \right)
\tag{2.48}\]

The eigenvector \(\left\vert  {{a_i}} \right\rangle\) of \(\hat A\) has the following column representation in its own eigenbasis:

\[
\lvert a_i\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}\langle a_1\vert a_i\rangle\\\vdots\\\langle a_i\vert a_i\rangle\\\vdots\\\langle a_N\vert a_i\rangle\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\\vdots\\1\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{(1 in row }i\text{)}
\tag{2.49}\]

An arbitrary Hermitian operator \(\hat B\) has the following matrix in the \(\hat A\) representation:

\[
\hat B = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\left\langle {{a_1}} \right\vert \hat B\left\vert  {{a_1}} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {{a_1}} \right\vert \hat B\left\vert  {{a_2}} \right\rangle }& \cdots \\ {\left\langle {{a_2}} \right\vert \hat B\left\vert  {{a_1}} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {{a_2}} \right\vert \hat B\left\vert  {{a_2}} \right\rangle }& \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{array}} \right)
\tag{2.50}\]

The matrix of \(\hat A\) in its own representation is diagonal, with the eigenvalues of \(\hat A\) on the diagonal:

\[
\hat A = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\left\langle {{a_1}} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {{a_1}} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {{a_1}} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {{a_2}} \right\rangle }& \cdots \\ {\left\langle {{a_2}} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {{a_1}} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {{a_2}} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {{a_2}} \right\rangle }& \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{a_1}}&0& \cdots \\ 0&{{a_2}}& \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{array}} \right)
\tag{2.51}\]

title: 2  Operators
text:
2.8 Exercises
2.1. Let {\(\left\vert  U \right\rangle ,\left\vert  D \right\rangle\)} be an orthonormal basis of a two-dimensional vector space. The two basis vectors have the following matrices in this basis:
\[
\vert U\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\langle U\vert U\rangle }\\ {\langle D\vert U\rangle } \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1\\ 0 \end{array}} \right), \qquad  \vert D\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\langle U\vert D\rangle }\\ {\langle D\vert D\rangle } \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0\\ 1 \end{array}} \right),
\tag{2.52}\]
Three operators \(\hat A,\hat B,\hat C\) in this space have the following properties:
\[
\begin{array}{l} \hat A\vert U\rangle = \vert D\rangle , & \hat A\vert D\rangle = \vert U\rangle \\ \hat B\vert U\rangle = i\vert D\rangle , & \hat B\vert D\rangle = - i\vert U\rangle \\ \hat C\vert U\rangle = \vert U\rangle , & \hat C\vert D\rangle = \vert D\rangle \end{array}
\tag{2.53}\]
Write the matrix of each operator in this basis. Hint: column 1 contains the components of the output for \(|U\rangle\), and column 2 contains the components of the output for \(|D\rangle\).
2.2. Let \(\left\vert  1 \right\rangle ,\left\vert  2 \right\rangle\) be an orthonormal basis of a two-dimensional space, with operator \(\hat H\) given by
\[
\hat H = \cos \theta \left\vert  1 \right\rangle \left\langle 1 \right\vert  + \sin \theta \left\vert  1 \right\rangle \left\langle 2 \right\vert  + \sin \theta \left\vert  2 \right\rangle \left\langle 1 \right\vert  - \cos \theta \left\vert  2 \right\rangle \left\langle 2 \right\vert
\tag{2.54}\]
Find the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenstates of \(\hat H\).
2.3. A Hermitian operator \(\hat A\) has nondegenerate eigenvalues \(\left\{ {{a_i}} \right\}\) and eigenstates \(\left\{ {\left\vert  {{a_i}} \right\rangle } \right\}\). Assume that none of the eigenvalues is zero, so that the inverse exists. Find the eigenvalues and eigenstates of \({\hat A^{ - 1}}\).
2.4. Prove that if \(\hat A\) is Hermitian, the eigenvalues of \({\hat A^2}\) are nonnegative.
2.5. Prove that \(\hat A{\hat A^\dagger }\) is Hermitian for any operator \(\hat A\).

title: 2  Operators
text: For a composite system, kets belonging to the state spaces of its separate subsystems can be combined into a tensor-product state, written \(|\psi\rangle\otimes|\phi\rangle\) or, when the meaning is clear, \(|\psi\rangle|\phi\rangle\). See Chapter 9.↩︎

title: 3  Quantum Measurement
text:
3.1 The measurement postulates
The previous chapters introduced state vectors and operators. We now use them to predict measurement outcomes: which values can occur, how likely each value is, and what state remains after a measurement. Spin-\(1/2\) provides a concrete example.
We begin with pure states and ideal projective measurements of observables with discrete spectra. Unless stated otherwise, the eigenvalues are nondegenerate and the eigenstates form a complete orthonormal basis.
To apply the measurement principle, solve \(\hat A\lvert a_j\rangle=a_j\lvert a_j\rangle\) for the eigenvalues and normalized eigenstates. For an initial state \(\lvert\psi\rangle\), the possible outcomes and the corresponding states are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{Result} & \text{State immediately after measurement} & \text{Probability} \\
\hline
a_1 & \lvert a_1\rangle & \lvert\langle a_1\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
a_j & \lvert a_j\rangle & \lvert\langle a_j\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots
\end{array}
\tag{3.1}\]
The outcome is generally random: the state determines the probabilities, but does not specify which outcome occurs in a particular trial. If the initial state is already an eigenstate \(\lvert a\rangle\), the outcome is certainly \(a\) and an ideal measurement leaves the physical state unchanged. An immediate repetition therefore gives the same result, provided no intervening evolution or measurement changes the state.
Measuring \(\hat A\) must yield some eigenvalue of \(\hat A\), so the probabilities sum to \(1\):
\[
\sum_j p(a_j)=\sum_j\lvert\langle a_j\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2=1
\tag{3.2}\] Equivalently, \[
\sum_j\langle\psi\vert a_j\rangle\langle a_j\vert\psi\rangle=1
\tag{3.3}\] By completeness, Equation 2.26, this simplifies to \[
\langle\psi\vert\psi\rangle=1
\tag{3.4}\] Normalization ensures that the probabilities of all possible outcomes sum to one.
For a degenerate eigenvalue \(a\), an ideal projective measurement uses the projector \(\hat P_a\) onto the whole eigenspace: \(p(a)=\langle\psi\vert\hat P_a\vert\psi\rangle\). Conditional on this outcome, the state becomes \(\hat P_a\lvert\psi\rangle/\sqrt{p(a)}\). Obtaining \(a\) need not select a unique eigenvector within that eigenspace.
The postulates also imply the following.
Theorem 3.1. In a normalized state \(\lvert\psi\rangle\), the expectation value of \(\hat A\) is \(\langle\hat A\rangle=\langle\psi\vert\hat A\vert\psi\rangle\). This is the average of measurements on many systems prepared in the same initial state; it need not itself be a possible outcome.
Proof.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle\psi\vert\hat A\vert\psi\rangle
&=\sum_i\langle\psi\vert\hat A\vert a_i\rangle\langle a_i\vert\psi\rangle \\
&=\sum_i a_i\langle\psi\vert a_i\rangle\langle a_i\vert\psi\rangle \\
&=\sum_i a_i\lvert\langle a_i\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2
=\sum_i a_i p(a_i).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.5}\] The final expression is the probability-weighted average of all outcomes, proving the theorem. We write \(\langle\hat A\rangle\) when the state is understood. Repeated measurements on a single system generally do not sample the initial distribution, because the first measurement changes its state.

title: 3  Quantum Measurement
text:
Quantum postulate 1—observables. An observable is represented by a Hermitian operator \(\hat A\). Its eigenvalues are the possible measurement outcomes.
Quantum postulate 2—states. A pure state is represented by a normalized vector \(\lvert\psi\rangle\), with \(\langle\psi\vert\psi\rangle=1\). This vector determines the probabilities of all measurement outcomes. Vectors \(e^{i\alpha}\lvert\psi\rangle\) and \(\lvert\psi\rangle\) represent the same physical state: an overall phase has no observable effect.
Quantum postulate 3—superposition. Any nonzero linear combination of allowed state vectors is also an allowed state vector after normalization. In an orthonormal basis \(\{\lvert\psi_j\rangle\}\), the superposition \(\sum_j c_j\lvert\psi_j\rangle\) is normalized when \(\sum_j\lvert c_j\rvert^2=1\).
Quantum postulate 4—definite values. An observable \(\hat A\) has a definite value \(a\) in a state if and only if that state lies in the eigenspace with eigenvalue \(a\). For a nondegenerate eigenvalue, this means the state is \(\lvert a\rangle\), up to an overall phase.
Quantum postulate 5—the measurement principle. Measuring \(\hat A\) in a normalized state \(\lvert\psi\rangle\) yields \(a_j\) with probability \(p(a_j)=\lvert\langle a_j\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2\). Immediately after an ideal measurement that gives \(a_j\), the state is \(\lvert a_j\rangle\), up to an overall phase. The overlap \(\langle a_j\vert\psi\rangle\) is the probability amplitude. More generally, \(\lvert\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle\rvert^2\) is the probability that a projective test for the normalized state \(\lvert\phi\rangle\) succeeds when the initial state is \(\lvert\psi\rangle\).









State preparation. Keeping only systems for which the measurement gives \(a_j\) prepares the state \(\lvert a_j\rangle\). This selection is called postselection.
Distinguishability. Two pure states can be distinguished with certainty in a single trial only if they are orthogonal. Orthogonal states can be included in an orthonormal measurement basis.
Sequential measurements. Starting in \(\lvert a\rangle\), the probability of obtaining \(b\) when measuring \(\hat B\) is \(\lvert\langle b\vert a\rangle\rvert^2\). If that outcome occurs, the state becomes \(\lvert b\rangle\), so a subsequent measurement of \(\hat A\) returns \(a\) with probability \(\lvert\langle a\vert b\rangle\rvert^2\). The joint probability of both outcomes is the product of these two probabilities. We assume ideal measurements and no evolution between them.

title: 3  Quantum Measurement
text:
3.2 A two-state spin system
A two-state system has a two-dimensional state space: two orthonormal basis states suffice to describe every state, although there are infinitely many superpositions. The spin state of a spin-\(1/2\) particle is an example. Write \(\hat\sigma_n=\hat{\boldsymbol\sigma}\cdot\mathbf n\), where \(\mathbf n\) is a spatial unit vector and \(\hat{\boldsymbol\sigma}=2\hat{\mathbf S}/\hbar\). Thus \(\hat\sigma_n\) is a dimensionless spin component; the physical component \(\hat S_n=(\hbar/2)\hat\sigma_n\) has outcomes \(\pm\hbar/2\).

Experiment: measuring \({\hat \sigma _n}\) yields either \(+ 1\) or \(- 1\).
Postulate: a measurement of an observable always yields one of its eigenvalues.
Conclusion: \({\hat \sigma _n}\) has only two eigenvalues, \(+ 1\) and \(- 1\). Assuming each is nondegenerate, call their eigenstates \(\left\vert  {\hat n + } \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  {\hat n - } \right\rangle\):

\[
{\hat \sigma _n}\left\vert  {\hat n + } \right\rangle = + \left\vert  {\hat n + } \right\rangle , \qquad  \qquad  {\hat \sigma _n}\left\vert  {\hat n - } \right\rangle = - \left\vert  {\hat n - } \right\rangle
\tag{3.6}\]
The eigenvalues differ, so \(\left\langle {{\hat n + }} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{\hat n + } {\hat n - }}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\hat n - }} \right\rangle = 0\). These normalized eigenstates form an orthonormal basis. Expressing states and operators in this basis defines the \({\hat \sigma _n}\) representation.
We give the states memorable names. In the coordinates of Figure 3.1, the states for \({\sigma _z} = + 1\) and \(- 1\) are \(\left\vert  U \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  D \right\rangle\) (Up and Down); those for \({\sigma _x} = + 1\) and \(- 1\) are \(\left\vert  R \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  L \right\rangle\) (Right and Left). Measuring the projection along \(y\), we call the states for \({\sigma _y} = + 1\) and \(- 1\) \(\left\vert  I \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  O \right\rangle\) (In and Out).


Figure 3.1. Coordinates defining Up and Down, Left and Right, and In and Out.

The eigenstates of \({\hat \sigma _z}\) are \(\left\vert  U \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  D \right\rangle\), with eigenvalues \(+ 1\) and \(- 1\), respectively. Hence
\[
{\hat \sigma _z}\left\vert  U \right\rangle = + \left\vert  U \right\rangle , \qquad  \qquad  {\hat \sigma _z}\left\vert  D \right\rangle = - \left\vert  D \right\rangle , \qquad  \qquad  \left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U D}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {D} \right\rangle = 0
\tag{3.7}\] Similarly, for \({\hat \sigma _x}\) and \({\hat \sigma _y}\),
\[
{\hat \sigma _x}\left\vert  R \right\rangle = + \left\vert  R \right\rangle , \qquad  \qquad  {\hat \sigma _x}\left\vert  L \right\rangle = - \left\vert  L \right\rangle , \qquad  \qquad  \left\langle {R} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {R L}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {L} \right\rangle = 0
\tag{3.8}\]
\[
{\hat \sigma _y}\left\vert  I \right\rangle = + \left\vert  I \right\rangle , \qquad  \qquad  {\hat \sigma _y}\left\vert  O \right\rangle = - \left\vert  O \right\rangle , \qquad  \qquad  \left\langle {I} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {I O}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {O} \right\rangle = 0
\tag{3.9}\]
To explain the experiments, we must now determine the relationships between these different states.

title: 3  Quantum Measurement
text:
3.3 Superposition of quantum states

3.3.1 Choosing a basis
We begin with eigenstates of different observables. In a spin-\(1/2\) state space, at most two states can be mutually orthogonal, such as \(\left\vert  U \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  D \right\rangle\), \(\left\vert  R \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  L \right\rangle\), or \(\left\vert  I \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  O \right\rangle\). Choosing the \({\hat \sigma _z}\) representation with basis \(\left\vert  U \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  D \right\rangle\), completeness Equation 2.26 gives
\[
\left\vert  U \right\rangle \left\langle U \right\vert  + \left\vert  D \right\rangle \left\langle D \right\vert  = \hat I
\tag{3.10}\] Any spin state \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) is a linear combination of \(\left\vert  U \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  D \right\rangle\). Following Equation 1.25,
\[
\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \left\vert  U \right\rangle \left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle + \left\vert  D \right\rangle \left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle
\tag{3.11}\]


3.3.2 States for measurements along \(x\)
To express \(\left\vert  R \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  L \right\rangle\) in basis \(\left\{ {\left\vert  U \right\rangle ,\left\vert  D \right\rangle } \right\}\), use Equation 3.11:
\[
\begin{array}{l} \left\vert  R \right\rangle = \left\vert  U \right\rangle \left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle + \left\vert  D \right\rangle \left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle \\ \left\vert  L \right\rangle = \left\vert  U \right\rangle \left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U L}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {L} \right\rangle + \left\vert  D \right\rangle \left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D L}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {L} \right\rangle \end{array}
\tag{3.12}\] In a Stern–Gerlach (SG) experiment, a system prepared in \(\lvert R\rangle\) has the definite value \(\sigma_x=+1\). A measurement along \(z\) then gives \(+1\) or \(-1\) with probability \(1/2\) each. Therefore,
\[\begin{equation}
{\left\vert  {\left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = {\left\vert  {\left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = 1/2
\end{equation}
\tag{3.13}\]
The general solution is \[
\left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}{e^{i{\phi _U}}}, \qquad  \qquad  \left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}{e^{i{\phi _D}}}
\tag{3.14}\] The angles \({\phi _U}\) and \({\phi _D}\) are undetermined phases. The expansion of \(\left\vert  R \right\rangle\) is therefore \[
\left\vert  R \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\left\vert  U \right\rangle + {e^{i\delta }}\left\vert  D \right\rangle } \right){e^{i{\phi _U}}}
\tag{3.15}\] Here \(\delta = {\phi _D} - {\phi _U}\). Since an overall phase is arbitrary, choose \({\phi _U} = 0\), or \({e^{i{\phi _U}}} = 1\), giving
\[
\left\vert  R \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\left\vert  U \right\rangle + {e^{i\delta }}\left\vert  D \right\rangle } \right)
\tag{3.16}\] The relative phase \(e^{i\delta}\) is not fixed by the \(z\)-measurement probabilities. Once the laboratory axes are fixed, however, it is not a freely adjustable physical property of \(\lvert R\rangle\). We may choose the phases of the basis vectors \(\lvert U\rangle\) and \(\lvert D\rangle\) so that this particular state has real, positive coefficients. With that basis convention, \(\delta=0\), giving
\[
\left\vert  R \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\left\vert  U \right\rangle + \left\vert  D \right\rangle } \right)
\tag{3.17}\] That is, \[
\left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}, \qquad  \left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}
\tag{3.18}\] Next express \(\left\vert  L \right\rangle\) in the \({\hat \sigma _z}\) representation. Using \(\left\langle {L} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {L R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle = 0\) and \(\left\langle {L} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {L L}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {L} \right\rangle = 1\), and setting an irrelevant overall phase to \(1\), gives \[
\left\vert  L \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\left\vert  U \right\rangle - \left\vert  D \right\rangle } \right)
\tag{3.19}\] The states \(\lvert R\rangle\) and \(\lvert L\rangle\) give identical probabilities for a \(z\) measurement, but opposite definite outcomes for an \(x\) measurement. The relative sign therefore matters physically. A coherent superposition is different from a statistical mixture: a 50:50 mixture of \(U\) and \(D\) gives both \(x\) outcomes with equal probability, whereas \(\lvert R\rangle\) gives \(+1\) with certainty.
Equations Equation 3.17 and Equation 3.19 expand \(\left\vert  R \right\rangle {\rm{,}}\left\vert  L \right\rangle\) in the \({\hat \sigma _z}\) representation. Inverting them gives the expansion of \(\left\vert  U \right\rangle {\rm{,}}\left\vert  D \right\rangle\) in the \({\hat \sigma _x}\) representation:
\[ \left\vert  U \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\left\vert  R \right\rangle + \left\vert  L \right\rangle } \right), \qquad  \qquad  \left\vert  D \right\rangle = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\left\vert  R \right\rangle - \left\vert  L \right\rangle } \right) \] Thus, when \({\sigma _z}\) is definitely \(+ 1\) or \(- 1\), a measurement of \({\sigma _x}\) yields \(+ 1\) and \(- 1\) with equal 50% probabilities, agreeing with experiment.


3.3.3 States for measurements along \(y\)
Finally, express the eigenstates \(\left\vert  I \right\rangle\) and \(\left\vert  O \right\rangle\) of \({\hat \sigma _y}\) in the \({\hat \sigma _z}\) representation. In an eigenstate of \({\hat \sigma _z}\), measurements of \({\hat \sigma _y}\) and \({\hat \sigma _x}\) are symmetric, so, as in Equation 3.13,
\[
{\left\vert  {\left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U I}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {I} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = {\left\vert  {\left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D I}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {I} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = \frac{1}{2}
