title: 4  Commutation Relations of Observables
text:
4.4 Measurement paths and interference
We have seen how an incompatible measurement can change later outcomes. Now consider a subtler question: what if an intermediate device offers several paths, and we allow them all to reach the final apparatus? The answer depends on whether the paths leave distinguishable records.
For a selected sequence of ideal measurement outcomes, conditional probabilities multiply. For coherent alternatives that reach the same final outcome without a path record, probability amplitudes add before we take the squared magnitude. The spin experiments let us compare these two situations explicitly.

4.4.1 A selected intermediate outcome
\[
\boxed{\hat A}\xrightarrow{\lvert a\prime\rangle}\boxed{\hat B}\xrightarrow{\lvert b\prime\rangle}\boxed{\hat A}\xrightarrow{\lvert a\prime\prime\rangle}
\tag{4.26}\]
Figure 4.7. A selected sequence of measurement outcomes; other channels are blocked.
Let \(\hat A\) and \(\hat B\) be incompatible observables with complete, nondegenerate eigenbases. The first measurement prepares \(\lvert a'\rangle\). Selecting the intermediate outcome \(b'\) then has probability \(\lvert\langle b'\vert a'\rangle\rvert^2\) and prepares \(\lvert b'\rangle\). The final outcome \(a''\) has conditional probability \(\lvert\langle a''\vert b'\rangle\rvert^2\). Given the initial preparation, the probability of this selected sequence is therefore
\[
{\left\vert  {\left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} \times {\left\vert  {\left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2}
\tag{4.27}\]
\[
\boxed{\hat A}\xrightarrow{\lvert a\prime\rangle}\boxed{\hat B}\xrightarrow{\text{all channels open}}\boxed{\hat A}\xrightarrow{\lvert a\prime\prime\rangle}
\tag{4.28}\]
Figure 4.8. All intermediate channels are open.


4.4.2 Open channels: recorded or coherently recombined?
Figure 4.8 leaves all intermediate channels open, but that alone does not specify the final probability. First suppose \(\hat B\) is actually measured, or a distinguishable record of its outcome is retained by a detector or the environment. Even if we ignore that record, the alternatives form a statistical mixture. The final probability is the sum of the probabilities for the separate sequences:
\[
\sum\limits_{b'} {{{\left\vert  {\left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle } \right\vert }^2}{{\left\vert  {\left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle } \right\vert }^2}} = \sum\limits_{b'} {\left\langle {{a'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a'} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a''}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a''}} \right\rangle }
\tag{4.29}\]
Now consider a different arrangement: the intermediate device separates the \(B\) channels, then recombines them coherently, preserving their relative phases and leaving no distinguishable path record. In the ideal arrangement considered here, separation and recombination introduce no net relative phase or other change of state.
For a single path, the amplitude is the product of its step amplitudes. For indistinguishable alternatives, we sum these products and then square the magnitude. Complex phases survive that sum and allow interference.
The total amplitude for Figure 4.7 is \(\left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle\), so its probability is
\[
{\left\vert  {\left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = {\left\vert  {\left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} \times {\left\vert  {\left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2}
\tag{4.30}\]
For one selected path, this reproduces Equation 4.27. For the coherently recombined arrangement in Figure 4.8, we instead sum over the intermediate paths. Completeness of the \(B\) basis, \(\sum_{b'}\lvert b'\rangle\langle b'\rvert=\hat I\), gives
\[
\sum\limits_{b'} {\left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle } = \sum\limits_{b'} {\left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {b'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{b'}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{b'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{b'} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle } = \left\langle {{a''}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{a''} {a'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{a'}} \right\rangle
\tag{4.31}\]
The probability is therefore \(\lvert\langle a''\vert a'\rangle\rvert^2\), just as if the intermediate apparatus were absent. This result depends on coherent recombination; an unread intermediate measurement gives the probability sum in Equation 4.29 instead.


4.4.3 Spin paths that cancel
Interpret the final experiment in Figure 1.2 as this ideal coherent arrangement. A particle prepared in \(\lvert U\rangle\) travels through the \(R\) and \(L\) channels of a \(\hat\sigma_x\) device, which are recombined before the final \(\hat\sigma_z\) measurement. No distinguishable path record remains. The probability of returning to \(\lvert U\rangle\) is
\[
{\left\vert  {\left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U U}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {U} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = 1
\tag{4.32}\]
Similarly, the probability of \(\left\vert  D \right\rangle\) is
\[
{\left\vert  {\left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D U}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {U} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = 0
\tag{4.33}\]
These results also follow by evaluating each path amplitude. For example, the probability of final state \(\left\vert  D \right\rangle\) is
\[
{\left\vert  {\left\langle {R} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {R U}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {U} \right\rangle \left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle + \left\langle {L} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {L U}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {U} \right\rangle \left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D L}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {L} \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = {\left\vert  {\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }} + \left( { - \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}} \right)\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}} \right\vert ^2} = 0
\tag{4.34}\]
Each path contributes a nonzero amplitude to \(\lvert D\rangle\), but the two contributions have opposite signs. Their sum vanishes: destructive interference removes the \(D\) outcome. If the intermediate \(x\) outcome were recorded instead, each path would contribute a probability of \(1/4\), so the final probabilities would be \(P(D)=P(U)=1/2\). The relative sign matters only when the amplitudes can interfere.
In classical optics, intensity at a screen point is proportional to the squared magnitude of the sum of electric fields arriving by different paths. Their relative phases produce constructive or destructive interference. The analogous relation between quantum probabilities and amplitudes motivates the description of quantum behavior as wave behavior.
The deciding question is whether a distinguishable path record remains, rather than whether anyone reads it. A detector or the environment can retain such a record and suppress interference through decoherence. Conversely, a microscopic particle can also lose coherence, and suitably isolated larger systems can display interference. Throughout, the same quantum rules apply: add probabilities for alternatives with distinguishable records, and add amplitudes for coherent alternatives.

title: 4  Commutation Relations of Observables
text:
4.5 Changing representations
The path amplitudes above are overlaps between two bases. Those same overlaps tell us how to rewrite a state in another representation. Chapter 3 used the \(\hat\sigma_z\) eigenbasis \(\{\lvert U\rangle,\lvert D\rangle\}\); we could equally use the \(\hat\sigma_x\) eigenbasis \(\{\lvert R\rangle,\lvert L\rangle\}\). The physical state stays the same, while its components in the chosen basis change—much as a spatial vector has different components along rotated Cartesian axes.

4.5.1 Transformation rules
Let \(\{\lvert a_i\rangle\}\) and \(\{\lvert b_i\rangle\}\) be two complete orthonormal bases of the same space. They may be eigenbases of incompatible observables, but the transformation rules do not require incompatibility. Fix an ordering for each basis and define an operator that maps corresponding basis vectors:
\[
\hat U\left\vert  {{a_j}} \right\rangle = \left\vert  {{b_j}} \right\rangle
\tag{4.35}\]
The outer-product expression makes this mapping explicit: when it acts on \(\lvert a_j\rangle\), orthonormality selects the term with \(i=j\).
\[
\hat U = \sum\limits_i {\left\vert  {{b_i}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{a_i}} \right\vert }
\tag{4.36}\]
By Equation 2.39,
\[
{\hat U^\dagger } = \sum\limits_i {\left\vert  {{a_i}} \right\rangle } \left\langle {{b_i}} \right\vert
\tag{4.37}\]
Acting on \(\lvert b_j\rangle\) shows that the adjoint reverses the mapping:
\[
{\hat U^\dagger }\left\vert  {{b_j}} \right\rangle = \left\vert  {{a_j}} \right\rangle
\tag{4.38}\]
Thus \({\hat U^\dagger }\) transforms the representation \(\hat B \to \hat A\). Combining Equation 4.36 and Equation 4.37 gives
\[
\hat U{\hat U^\dagger } = {\hat U^\dagger }\hat U = \hat I
\tag{4.39}\]
Thus \(\hat U\) is unitary, with \(\hat U^{-1}=\hat U^\dagger\). Unitary transformations preserve inner products and norms. This is exactly what a change of orthonormal basis must do: probabilities cannot depend on which basis we use to calculate them.
Keep two operations distinct. The operator \(\hat U\) maps basis kets to new basis kets. Re-expressing the same physical state in the new basis will require the inverse matrix. We derive that rule below.
The matrix elements of transformation operator \(\hat U\) in the \(\hat A\) representation are
\[
\langle {{a_l}}\vert {\hat U}\vert {{a_m}}\rangle = \sum\limits_i {\left\langle {{a_l}} \right.\left\vert  {{b_i}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{a_i}} \right\vert } \left. {{a_m}} \right\rangle = \sum\limits_i {\left\langle {{a_l}} \right.\left\vert  {{b_i}} \right\rangle {\delta _{im}}} = \left\langle {{a_l}} \right.\left\vert  {{b_m}} \right\rangle
\tag{4.40}\]
The elements of \(\hat U\) in the \(\hat B\) representation are
\[
\langle b_l\vert\hat U\vert b_m\rangle
=\sum_i\langle b_l\vert b_i\rangle\langle a_i\vert b_m\rangle
=\sum_i\delta_{li}\langle a_i\vert b_m\rangle
=\langle a_l\vert b_m\rangle
\tag{4.41}\]
With the corresponding ordering, this particular mapping operator has the same matrix in the two chosen bases. Its columns are the new basis vectors expressed in the old basis:
\[
\hat U \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\left\langle {{{a_1}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_1}} {{b_1}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{b_1}}} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {{{a_1}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_1}} {{b_2}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{b_2}}} \right\rangle }& \cdots \\ {\left\langle {{{a_2}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_2}} {{b_1}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{b_1}}} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {{{a_2}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_2}} {{b_2}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{b_2}}} \right\rangle }& \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{array}} \right)
\tag{4.42}\]
Likewise, the inverse \({\hat U^\dagger }\) has the same matrix in both:
\[
\hat U_{ij}^\dagger = {\left( {{{\hat U}_{ji}}} \right)^*} = \left\langle {{{b_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_i}} {{a_j}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{a_j}}} \right\rangle
\tag{4.43}\]
To express a state vector in the new basis, insert the identity \(\sum_j\lvert a_j\rangle\langle a_j\rvert\) into \(\langle b_i\vert\psi\rangle\). This expresses each new component as a sum of old components weighted by basis overlaps:
\[
\left\langle {{{b_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_i}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle = \sum\limits_j {\left\langle {{{b_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_i}} {{a_j}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{a_j}}} \right\rangle } \left\langle {{{a_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_j}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle = \sum\limits_j {\left\langle {{a_i}} \right\vert {{\hat U}^\dagger }\left\vert  {{a_j}} \right\rangle } \left\langle {{{a_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_j}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle
\tag{4.44}\]
Therefore,
\[
\left( \begin{array}{c} \left\langle {{{b_1}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_1}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle \\ \left\langle {{{b_2}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_2}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle \\ \vdots \end{array} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\left\langle {{{b_1}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_1}} {{a_1}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{a_1}}} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {{{b_1}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_1}} {{a_2}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{a_2}}} \right\rangle }& \cdots \\ {\left\langle {{{b_2}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_2}} {{a_1}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{a_1}}} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {{{b_2}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_2}} {{a_2}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{a_2}}} \right\rangle }& \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{array}} \right)\left( \begin{array}{c} \left\langle {{{a_1}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_1}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle \\ \left\langle {{{a_2}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_2}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle \\ \vdots \end{array} \right)
\tag{4.45}\]
The left-hand column contains the components of \(\lvert\psi\rangle\) in the \(B\) basis. The right-hand column contains its components in the \(A\) basis, multiplied by the overlap matrix with elements \(\langle b_i\vert a_j\rangle\). That matrix is \(\hat U^\dagger\), so
\[
{\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle _B} = {\hat U^\dagger }{\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle _A}
\tag{4.46}\]
For an operator, the corresponding transformation is
\[
\begin{array}{c} \left\langle {{b_i}} \right\vert \hat X\left\vert  {{b_j}} \right\rangle = \sum\limits_{l,m} {\left\langle {{{b_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{b_i}} {{a_l}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{a_l}}} \right\rangle } \left\langle {{a_l}} \right\vert \hat X\left\vert  {{a_m}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{a_m}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{a_m}} {{b_j}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{b_j}}} \right\rangle \\ = \sum\limits_{l,m} {\left\langle {{a_i}} \right\vert {{\hat U}^\dagger }\left\vert  {{a_l}} \right\rangle } \left\langle {{a_l}} \right\vert \hat X\left\vert  {{a_m}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{a_m}} \right\vert \hat U\left\vert  {{a_j}} \right\rangle \end{array}
\tag{4.47}\]
The left side is the matrix of \(\hat X\) in the \(\hat B\) representation; the three factors on the right are the matrices of \({\hat U^\dagger },\hat X,\hat U\) in the \(\hat A\) representation. Hence
\[
{\hat X_B} = {\hat U^\dagger }{\hat X_A}\hat U
\tag{4.48}\]
Here the subscripts identify the bases used for the state-vector columns and operator matrices. The rule \(\hat X_B=\hat U^\dagger\hat X_A\hat U\) is a unitary similarity transformation: the factor on the right expresses the input state vector in the \(A\) basis, \(\hat X_A\) acts, and the factor on the left expresses the result in the \(B\) basis.
Example: view spin from the \(x\) basis. Find the matrices of \(\hat\sigma_x\), \(\hat\sigma_y\), and \(\hat\sigma_z\) in the \(\hat\sigma_x\) eigenbasis. We expect \(\hat\sigma_x\) to become diagonal, because the basis states have definite \(x\) spin.
The \({\hat \sigma _z}\) basis is \(\left\vert  U \right\rangle ,\left\vert  D \right\rangle\), and the \({\hat \sigma _x}\) basis is \(\left\vert  R \right\rangle ,\left\vert  L \right\rangle\). By Equation 4.42, the matrix of \(\hat U\) for the change \({\hat \sigma _z} \to {\hat \sigma _x}\) is
\[
\hat U \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {U} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {U L}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {L} \right\rangle }\\ {\left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D R}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {R} \right\rangle }&{\left\langle {D} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {D L}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {L} \right\rangle } \end{array}} \right) = \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&1\\ 1&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{4.49}\]
By Equation 4.43, its inverse \({\hat U^\dagger }\) has matrix
\[
{\hat U^\dagger } \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&1\\ 1&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{4.50}\]
Using Equation 4.48, in the \({\hat \sigma _x}\) representation we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{l} {{\hat \sigma }_x} \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&1\\ 1&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&1\\ 1&0 \end{array}} \right)\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&1\\ 1&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&0\\ 0&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right)\\ {{\hat \sigma }_y} \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&1\\ 1&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{ - i}\\ i&0 \end{array}} \right)\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&1\\ 1&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&i\\ { - i}&0 \end{array}} \right)\\ {{\hat \sigma }_z} \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&1\\ 1&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&0\\ 0&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right)\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&1\\ 1&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&1\\ 1&0 \end{array}} \right) \end{array}
\tag{4.51}\]
Theorem 4.3. An observable’s matrix has the same trace—the sum of diagonal elements—in every representation. It equals the sum of all eigenvalues, counting an eigenvalue of degeneracy \(n\) exactly \(n\) times.
\[
\sum\limits_i {\left\langle {{b_i}} \right\vert \hat X\left\vert  {{b_i}} \right\rangle } = \sum\limits_j {\left\langle {{a_j}} \right\vert \hat X\left\vert  {{a_j}} \right\rangle }
\tag{4.52}\]
Proof. Use Equation 4.48 and the trace identity \({\rm{Tr}}\left( {AB} \right) = {\rm{Tr}}\left( {BA} \right)\).
\[
{\text{Tr}}\left( {{{\hat X}_B}} \right) = {\text{Tr}}\;\left( {{{\hat U}^\dagger }{{\hat X}_A}\hat U} \right) = {\text{Tr}}\;\left( {\hat U{{\hat U}^\dagger }{{\hat X}_A}} \right) = {\text{Tr}}\left( {{{\hat X}_A}} \right)
\tag{4.53}\]
The trace is therefore independent of the basis. In an observable’s eigenbasis, its matrix is diagonal (Equation 2.56), so the trace is simply the eigenvalue sum, with repeated eigenvalues counted according to their degeneracy. A basis change rearranges the matrix elements while preserving this sum.


4.5.2 Eigenvalue equations and changes of basis
Suppose the matrix of \(\hat B\) is given in the \(A\) basis. Solve its eigenvalue equation there. Taking the overlap with \(\langle a_l\rvert\) gives
\[
\sum_i\langle a_l\vert\hat B\vert a_i\rangle
\langle a_i\vert b_m\rangle
=b_m\langle a_l\vert b_m\rangle
\tag{4.54}\] \(m\)th normalized eigenvector has components \(\langle a_i\vert b_m\rangle\)—exactly column \(m\) of \(\hat U\). Arrange an orthonormal set of these eigenvectors as columns. The resulting matrix is the \(\hat U\) that transforms \(\hat B_A\) to \(\hat U^\dagger\hat B_A\hat U=\hat B_B\), a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues \(b_m\). This is diagonalization.
If an eigenvalue is degenerate, choose an orthonormal basis within its eigenspace; the choice is not unique.


4.5.3 Summary of changes of representation
For quick reference, fix the convention \(\hat U\lvert a_j\rangle=\lvert b_j\rangle\). Its matrix columns are the new basis kets in the old basis, \(U_{ij}=\langle a_i\vert b_j\rangle\). Then:

Reverse the basis mapping: \(\lvert a_j\rangle=\hat U^\dagger\lvert b_j\rangle\).
Unitarity: \(\hat U\hat U^\dagger=\hat U^\dagger\hat U=\hat I\).
State vector in the new basis: \(\lvert\psi\rangle_B=\hat U^\dagger\lvert\psi\rangle_A\).
Operator matrices: \(\hat X_B=\hat U^\dagger\hat X_A\hat U\).

For the mapping operator defined here, its matrices in these two specifically paired bases agree, as do those of its adjoint. This does not mean that either matrix is the same in every possible representation:
\[
\begin{array}{l} \langle {{a_l}}\vert {\hat U}\vert {{a_m}}\rangle = \langle {{b_l}}\vert {\hat U}\vert {{b_m}}\rangle = \langle {{a_l}}\vert {{b_m}}\rangle \\ \langle {{a_l}}\vert {{{\hat U}^\dagger }}\vert {{a_m}}\rangle = \langle {{b_l}}\vert {{\hat U}^\dagger }\vert {{b_m}}\rangle = \langle {b_l}\vert {{a_m}}\rangle \end{array}
\tag{4.55}\]

title: 4  Commutation Relations of Observables
text:
4.6 * The Heisenberg uncertainty principle
Compatibility tells us when a common eigenbasis exists. Uncertainty quantifies the spread of outcomes in a particular state. A definite value has zero spread; a superposition of different eigenvalues generally does not. The commutator connects these two ideas.
For a normalized state \(\lvert\psi\rangle\), all expectation values in this section refer to that same preparation. Define the deviation operators \(\Delta\hat A=\hat A-\langle\hat A\rangle\hat I\) and \(\Delta\hat B=\hat B-\langle\hat B\rangle\hat I\). They subtract the mean from each observable.
The variance is \(\langle(\Delta\hat A)^2\rangle=\langle\hat A^2\rangle-\langle\hat A\rangle^2\). Its square root, \(\Delta A\), is the standard deviation of the measurement outcomes. Distinguish the number \(\Delta A\) from the operator \(\Delta\hat A\).
We will prove the Robertson uncertainty relation, often called the generalized Heisenberg uncertainty relation: \(\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\tfrac12\lvert\langle[\hat A,\hat B]\rangle\rvert\). The proof has three ingredients: subtract the means, apply the Schwarz inequality, and split the operator product into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts.
Proof. In addition to the commutator, define the anticommutator \(\{\hat X,\hat Y\}=\hat X\hat Y+\hat Y\hat X\). Any product separates into these two parts:
\[
\hat X\hat Y = \frac{1}{2}[\hat X,\hat Y] + \frac{1}{2}{\rm{\{ }}\hat X,\hat Y{\rm{\} }}
\tag{4.56}\]
Let \(\hat A,\hat B\) be Hermitian operators.
Taking adjoints reverses the order of a product. For Hermitian \(\hat A\) and \(\hat B\), this gives \([\hat A,\hat B]^\dagger=-[\hat A,\hat B]\) and \(\{\hat A,\hat B\}^\dagger=\{\hat A,\hat B\}\).
Consequently,
\[
\langle [\hat A,\hat B]\rangle \text{ is purely imaginary}, \qquad  \langle \{ \hat A,\hat B\} \rangle \text{ is real}
\tag{4.57}\]
Also,
\[
\langle [\Delta \hat A,\Delta \hat B]\rangle = \langle [\hat A,\hat B]\rangle , \qquad  \langle \{ \Delta \hat A,\Delta \hat B\} \rangle = \langle \{ \hat A,\hat B\} \rangle - 2\langle {\hat A}\rangle \langle {\hat B}\rangle
\tag{4.58}\]
Combining these gives
\[
\langle [\Delta \hat A,\Delta \hat B]\rangle = \langle [\hat A,\hat B]\rangle \;\text{ is purely imaginary}, \qquad  \langle \{ \Delta \hat A,\Delta \hat B\} \rangle \;\text{ is real}
\tag{4.59}\]
Substitute \(\hat X = \Delta \hat A,\;\hat Y = \Delta \hat B\) into Equation 4.56 and take expectation values:
\[
\langle {\Delta \hat A\Delta \hat B}\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\langle {[\Delta \hat A,\Delta \hat B]}\rangle + \frac{1}{2}\langle {{\rm{\{ }}\Delta \hat A,\Delta \hat B{\rm{\} }}}\rangle
\tag{4.60}\]
The Schwarz inequality states that for any states \(\vert \alpha \rangle ,\;\vert \beta \rangle\),
\[
\langle \alpha \vert \alpha \rangle \langle \beta \vert \beta \rangle \ge {\left\vert  {\langle \alpha \vert \beta \rangle } \right\vert ^2}
\tag{4.61}\]
Apply the Schwarz inequality to \(\lvert\alpha\rangle=\Delta\hat A\lvert\psi\rangle\) and \(\lvert\beta\rangle=\Delta\hat B\lvert\psi\rangle\). Their squared norms are the two variances. Their overlap is \(\langle\Delta\hat A\Delta\hat B\rangle\), whose real and imaginary parts come from the anticommutator and commutator respectively. Thus
\[
\langle {{{(\Delta \hat A)}^2}}\rangle \langle {{{(\Delta \hat B)}^2}}\rangle \ge {\left\vert  {\langle {\Delta \hat A\Delta \hat B}\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = {\left( {\frac{1}{{2i}}\langle [\hat A,\hat B]\rangle } \right)^2} + {\left( {\frac{1}{2}\langle \{ \Delta \hat A,\Delta \hat B\} \rangle } \right)^2}
\tag{4.62}\]
The second term on the right of Equation 4.62 is a real square and is nonnegative. Hence
\[
\langle {{{(\Delta \hat A)}^2}}\rangle \langle {{{(\Delta \hat B)}^2}}\rangle \ge \frac{1}{4}{\left( {i\langle [\hat A,\hat B]\rangle } \right)^2}
\tag{4.63}\]
Define the standard deviation \(\Delta A \equiv \sqrt {\langle {{{(\Delta \hat A)}^2}}\rangle }\) and take square roots to obtain the familiar uncertainty relation:
\[
\Delta A\Delta B \ge \frac{1}{2}\left\vert  {\langle [\hat A,\hat B]\rangle } \right\vert
\tag{4.64}\]
The relation describes statistical spreads in identically prepared systems. Determine \(\Delta A\) from repeated measurements of \(A\) on one ensemble and \(\Delta B\) from measurements of \(B\) on another ensemble with the same preparation. It does not, by itself, specify the disturbance caused by a sequential measurement.
For position and momentum, \([\hat x,\hat p_x]=i\hbar\hat I\) gives \(\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge\hbar/2\). For spin, \([\hat S_x,\hat S_y]=i\hbar\hat S_z\) gives \(\Delta S_x\,\Delta S_y\ge(\hbar/2)\lvert\langle\hat S_z\rangle\rvert\). In \(\lvert U\rangle\), both transverse standard deviations are \(\hbar/2\), and the inequality is saturated. Notice that the spin bound depends on the state: noncommuting observables can have a zero lower bound in a state where the commutator’s expectation vanishes.
Time is a parameter in this formulation, so an energy–time relation cannot be obtained simply by substituting a time operator into the result above. One precise version uses the time scale \(\tau_A=\Delta A/\lvert d\langle\hat A\rangle/dt\rvert\) for the mean of an observable with no explicit time dependence to change by one standard deviation. For unitary evolution with a time-independent Hamiltonian and a nonzero rate of change, the uncertainty relation and the equation of motion give \(\Delta E\,\tau_A\ge\hbar/2\). Here \(\tau_A\) is a dynamical time scale; the time-evolution chapter supplies the equation of motion.

title: 4  Commutation Relations of Observables
text:
4.7 Exercises
4.1. Define \({\rm{\{ }}\hat A,\hat B{\rm{\} }} \equiv \hat A\hat B + \hat B\hat A\). Prove \[
\hat A\hat B = \frac{1}{2}\left[ {\hat A,\hat B} \right] + \frac{1}{2}\left\{ {\hat A,\hat B} \right\}
\].
4.2. Eigenstates \(\vert {a_i}\rangle ,\vert {a_j}\rangle\) of \(\hat A\) have distinct eigenvalues \({a_i},{a_j}\). If \([\hat A,\hat B] = 0\), prove
\[
\langle {{a_i}}\vert {\hat B}\vert {{a_j}}\rangle = 0
\tag{4.65}\]
4.3. Using Equation 4.5 and Equation 4.6, prove the first relation below for angular momentum of any spin. For the second, specialize to the spin-\(1/2\) matrices in Equation 3.42:
\[
\left[ {{{{\bf{\hat S}}}^2},{{\hat S}_z}} \right] = 0, \qquad  \left[ {\hat S_x^2,\hat S_y^2} \right] = 0
\tag{4.66}\]
4.4. Prove that the mean of an anti-Hermitian operator, \({\hat C^\dagger } = - \hat C\), is purely imaginary.
4.5. Express \(\lvert R\rangle\) and \(\lvert L\rangle\) as column vectors, and \(\hat\sigma_x\) as a matrix, in the \(\hat\sigma_y\) eigenbasis.
4.6*. Let \(\langle\hat X\rangle\) denote the expectation value in a normalized state, and define \(\Delta\hat X=\hat X-\langle\hat X\rangle\hat I\). For Hermitian \(\hat A\) and \(\hat B\), prove:

\(\langle {[\hat A,\hat B]}\rangle\) is purely imaginary.
\(\langle {{\rm{\{ }}\Delta \hat A,\Delta \hat B{\rm{\} }}}\rangle\) is real.

title: 5  Time Evolution
text:
5.1 * Motivating the Schrödinger equation
So far we have discussed states at a given instant. Even sequences of measurements were implicitly performed immediately one after another, before appreciable evolution could occur. We now examine how a state changes with time.
Quantum postulate 6. Between measurements, a system’s state evolves according to the Schrödinger equation.
The Schrödinger equation plays the role in quantum mechanics that Newton’s second law plays in classical mechanics. It cannot be derived from more elementary principles within this presentation; its validity ultimately rests on experiment. Here we consider a modern route to deduce the equation.
An initial state \(\vert \psi (0)\rangle\) evolves after time \(t\) into \(\vert \psi (t)\rangle\). We seek the law governing this evolution:
\[
\left\vert  {\psi \left( 0 \right)} \right\rangle \xrightarrow{{\text{time evolution}}}\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle
\tag{5.1}\]
Since operator changes state, we introduce a time-evolution operator \(\hat U(t)\) relating the initial state to that after \(t\):
\[
\hat U\left( t \right)\left\vert  {\psi (0)} \right\rangle = \left\vert  {\psi (t)} \right\rangle
\tag{5.2}\]
Physical considerations impose three requirements.
First: as the elapsed time tends to zero, \(\hat U(t)\) leaves the state unchanged:
\[
\mathop {\lim }\limits_{t \to 0} \hat U\left( t \right) = \hat I
\tag{5.3}\]
Second: Time evolution of two successive intervals compose to give evolution over the combined interval.
\[
\hat U\left( {{t_2}} \right)\hat U\left( {{t_1}} \right)\left\vert  {\psi \left( 0 \right)} \right\rangle = \hat U\left( {{t_2}} \right)\left\vert  {\psi \left( {{t_1}} \right)} \right\rangle = \left\vert  {\psi \left( {{t_1} + {t_2}} \right)} \right\rangle = \hat U\left( {{t_1} + {t_2}} \right)\left\vert  {\psi \left( 0 \right)} \right\rangle
\tag{5.4}\]
Therefore,
\[
\hat U\left( {{t_2}} \right)\hat U\left( {{t_1}} \right) = \hat U\left( {{t_1} + {t_2}} \right) = \hat U\left( {{t_1}} \right)\hat U\left( {{t_2}} \right)
\tag{5.5}\]
Third: probability is conserved, \(\langle {\psi (t)}\vert {\psi (t)}\rangle = \langle {\psi (0)}\vert {\psi (0)}\rangle\), so
\[
{\hat U^\dagger }\left( t \right)\hat U\left( t \right) = \hat I
\tag{5.6}\]
Thus \(\hat U\) is unitary: time evolution is a unitary transformation.
These requirements suggest an infinitesimal evolution operator \(\hat U(dt)\):
\[
\hat U\left( {dt} \right)\left\vert  {\psi (0)} \right\rangle = \left\vert  {\psi (dt)} \right\rangle
\tag{5.7}\]
where
\[
\hat U\left( {dt} \right) \equiv \hat I - i\hat \Omega dt
\tag{5.8}\]
Neglecting higher-order terms in \(dt\), \(\hat U(dt)\) satisfies the first two requirements. The third gives
\[
\left( {\hat I{\rm{ + }}i{{\hat \Omega }^\dagger }dt} \right)\left( {\hat I - i\hat \Omega dt} \right) = I
\tag{5.9}\]
Expanding and neglecting higher-order terms in \(dt\),
\[
\hat I{\rm{ + }}idt\hat I\left( {{{\hat \Omega }^\dagger } - \hat \Omega } \right) = \hat I
\tag{5.10}\]
Hence
\[
\hat \Omega = {\hat \Omega ^\dagger }
\tag{5.11}\]
Thus \(\hat \Omega\) must be Hermitian, suggesting an observable. Equation Equation 5.8 shows that \(\hat \Omega\) has frequency dimensions. Classical frequency describes a rate of variation rather than a fundamental dynamical observable. Planck’s frequency–energy relation, however, gives
\[
E = \hbar \omega
\tag{5.12}\]
The energy operator, or Hamiltonian, is denoted \(\hat H\). We therefore propose
\[
\hat \Omega = {{\hat H} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{\hat H} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }
\tag{5.13}\]
The infinitesimal evolution operator becomes
\[
\hat U\left( {dt} \right) = \hat I - i\frac{{\hat H}}{\hbar }dt
\tag{5.14}\]
Because of the central role of \(\hat H\) in time evolution, it is called the generator of time evolution.
From \(\hat U(dt)\), we obtain a differential equation for \(\hat U(t)\), defined in Equation 5.2:
\[
\hat U\left( {t + dt} \right) = \hat U\left( {dt} \right)\hat U\left( t \right) = \left( {\hat I - i\frac{{\hat H}}{\hbar }dt} \right)\hat U\left( t \right)
\tag{5.15}\]
Thus,
\[
\frac{{\hat U\left( {t + dt} \right) - \hat U\left( t \right)}}{{dt}} = - i\frac{{\hat H}}{\hbar }\hat U\left( t \right)
\tag{5.16}\]
Multiplying by \(i\hbar\) gives
\[
i\hbar \frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\hat U\left( t \right) = \hat H\hat U\left( t \right)
\tag{5.17}\]
Equation Equation 5.17 is the Schrödinger equation for the evolution operator. Acting with both sides of Equation 5.16 on \(\vert \psi (0)\rangle\) gives the familiar state equation:
\[
i\hbar \frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle = \hat H\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle
\tag{5.18}\]

title: 5  Time Evolution
text:
5.2 Solving the Schrödinger equation
Here \(\vert \psi (t)\rangle\) is the state at time \(t\), and \(\hat H\) is the Hamiltonian. The equation describes state evolution and is first order in time, so only the initial condition \(\vert \psi (0)\rangle\) is needed. Knowing the Hamiltonian and the state at one instant determines all subsequent states.
Assume \(\hat H\) has no explicit time dependence. Then \(\hat H\) is constant in time, and \(\hat H\) has fixed eigenvalues \({E_j}\) and eigenvectors \(\vert {E_j}\rangle\):
\[
\hat H\left\vert  {{E_j}} \right\rangle = {E_j}\left\vert  {{E_j}} \right\rangle
\tag{5.19}\]
The energy eigenvalue equation is also called the time-independent Schrödinger equation. Energy is central to quantum mechanics: many problems reduce to constructing the Hamiltonian and finding its eigenvalues and eigenstates exactly or approximately.
Since the Schrödinger equation contains \(\hat H\), the \(\hat H\) representation is convenient. Multiply Equation 5.18 on the left by \(\langle {E_j}\vert\):
\[
i\hbar \frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi \left( t \right)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi \left( t \right)}} \right\rangle = \left\langle {{E_j}} \right\vert \hat H\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle = {E_j}\left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi \left( t \right)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi \left( t \right)}} \right\rangle
\tag{5.20}\]
This is a first-order differential equation for \(\langle {E_j}\vert \psi (t)\rangle\), with solution
\[
\left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi \left( t \right)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi \left( t \right)}} \right\rangle = \left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi \left( 0 \right)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi \left( 0 \right)}} \right\rangle {e^{ - {{i{E_j}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{E_j}t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}
\tag{5.21}\]
Hence the energy-basis expansion of \(\vert \psi (t)\rangle\) is
\[
\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle = \sum\limits_j {\left\vert  {{E_j}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi \left( t \right)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi \left( t \right)}} \right\rangle } = \sum\limits_j {\left\vert  {{E_j}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi \left( 0 \right)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi \left( 0 \right)}} \right\rangle {e^{ - {{i{E_j}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{E_j}t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}}
\tag{5.22}\]
This is the general solution for time-independent \(\hat H\). Comparing the initial and final expansions makes the result easy to remember.
\[
\begin{array}{c} \left\vert  {\psi \left( 0 \right)} \right\rangle = \sum\limits_j {\left\vert  {{E_j}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi \left( 0 \right)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi \left( 0 \right)}} \right\rangle } \\ \left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle = \sum\limits_j {\left\vert  {{E_j}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi \left( 0 \right)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi \left( 0 \right)}} \right\rangle {e^{ - {{i{E_j}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{E_j}t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}} \end{array}
\tag{5.23}\]

5.2.1 Stationary states
Suppose the initial state is an eigenstate of \(\hat H\):
\[
\left\vert  {\psi {\rm{(}}0)} \right\rangle = \left\vert  {{E_m}} \right\rangle
\tag{5.24}\]
Then Equation 5.22 becomes
\[
\begin{array}{c} \left\vert  {\psi (t)} \right\rangle = \sum\limits_j {\left\vert  {{E_j}} \right\rangle {\delta _{jm}}{e^{ - {{i{E_j}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{E_j}t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}} = \left\vert  {{E_m}} \right\rangle {e^{ - {{i{E_m}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{E_m}t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}\\ = {e^{ - {{i{E_m}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{E_m}t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}\left\vert  {\psi (0)} \right\rangle \end{array}
\tag{5.25}\]
The final vector differs from the initial one only by an overall phase, so they represent the same physical state. For a time-independent Hamiltonian, an initial energy eigenstate therefore remains physically unchanged and is called a stationary state. Since a state contains all information about the system, its time-independent physical properties remain unchanged.

title: 5  Time Evolution
text:
5.3 Time evolution of expectation values
Once the state evolution is known, the expectation value of any observable \(\hat A\) follows from \(\langle {\hat A(t)}\rangle \equiv \left\langle {\psi (t)} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {\psi (t)} \right\rangle\). Use Equation 5.23 to obtain \(\left\vert  {\psi (t)} \right\rangle\), then calculate \(\left\langle {\psi (t)} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {\psi (t)} \right\rangle\).
More generally, Equation 3.5 and Equation 5.23 give
\[
\begin{array}{c} \left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle = \sum\limits_{j,k} {{e^{{{i{E_j}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{E_j}t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}\left\langle {{\psi (0)}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{\psi (0)} {{E_j}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{E_j}}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{E_j}} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {{E_k}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{E_k}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_k}} {\psi (0)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi (0)}} \right\rangle {e^{{{ - i{E_k}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{ - i{E_k}t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}} \\ = \sum\limits_{j,k} {\left\langle {{\psi (0)}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{\psi (0)} {{E_j}}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{{E_j}}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{E_k}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_k}} {\psi (0)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi (0)}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{E_j}} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {{E_k}} \right\rangle {e^{{{i\left( {{E_j} - {E_k}} \right)t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i\left( {{E_j} - {E_k}} \right)t} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }}}} \end{array}
\tag{5.26}\]
Without the final time-dependent phase in each summand, this is the expectation of \(\hat A\) in initial state \(\vert {\psi (0)}\rangle\). If the initial state contains components \(\vert {E_j}\rangle\) and \(\vert {E_k}\rangle\) of different energies, with \(\left\langle {{{E_j}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_j}} {\psi (0)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi (0)}} \right\rangle\) and \(\left\langle {{{E_k}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{E_k}} {\psi (0)}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{\psi (0)}} \right\rangle\) both nonzero, and \(\hat A\) has nonzero matrix element \({A_{jk}} \equiv \left\langle {{E_j}} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {{E_k}} \right\rangle \ne 0\) between them, the mean of \(\hat A\) contains an oscillation at frequency \({\omega _{jk}} \equiv {{({E_j} - {E_k})} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{({E_j} - {E_k})} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }\). This offers a qualitative picture of atomic radiation: take \(\hat A\) to be electron position. If a perturbation mixes energy state \(\vert {E_k}\rangle\) into an initial eigenstate \(\vert {E_j}\rangle\), the mean position oscillates at \({\omega _{jk}}\), suggesting radiation at that frequency during a transition. Heisenberg arrived at Equation 5.26 while studying transitions and built matrix mechanics around this insight. The matrix form of Equation 5.26 is
\[
\left\langle {\psi (t)} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {\psi (t)} \right\rangle \buildrel\textstyle.\over= {\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\langle 1\vert {\psi (0)}\rangle }\\ {\langle 2\vert {\psi (0)}\rangle }\\ \vdots \\ \vdots \end{array}} \right)^\dagger }\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{l}} {{A_{11}}}&{{A_{12}}{e^{i{\omega _{12}}t}}}&{{A_{13}}{e^{{\omega _{13}}t}}}& \cdots \\ {{A_{21}}{e^{i{\omega _{21}}t}}}&{{A_{22}}}&{{A_{23}}{e^{{\omega _{23}}t}}}& \cdots \\ {{A_{31}}{e^{i{\omega _{31}}t}}}&{{A_{32}}{e^{{\omega _{32}}t}}}&{{A_{33}}}& \cdots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\langle 1\vert {\psi (0)}\rangle }\\ {\langle 2\vert {\psi (0)}\rangle }\\ \vdots \\ \vdots \end{array}} \right)
\tag{5.27}\]
If \(\hat A\) has no explicit time dependence, there is a direct way to find the evolution of \(\left\langle {\psi (t)} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {\psi (t)} \right\rangle\).
First write the Schrödinger equation in the bra space:
\[
- i\hbar \frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert  = \left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert \hat H
\tag{5.28}\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{array}{c} \frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle = \left( {\frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert } \right)\hat A\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle + \left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert \hat A\frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle \\ = \frac{{ - 1}}{{i\hbar }}\left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert \hat H\hat A\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle + \frac{1}{{i\hbar }}\left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert \hat A\hat H\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle \end{array}
\tag{5.29}\]
Multiply by \(i\hbar\) to obtain
\[
i\hbar \frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle = \left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert [\hat A,\hat H]\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle
\tag{5.30}\]
This is often abbreviated as
\[
i\hbar \frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\langle \hat A(t)\rangle = \langle [\hat A,\hat H]\rangle
\tag{5.31}\]

title: 5  Time Evolution
text:
5.4 Constants of motion
By Equation 5.30, if \(\hat A\) has no explicit time dependence and commutes with the Hamiltonian,
\[
\frac{\partial }{{\partial t}}\left\langle {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\vert \hat A\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle = 0
\tag{5.32}\]
The mean of \(\hat A\) is constant. If \(\hat A\) initially has a definite value, that value equals its mean and \(\hat A\) retains it.
An observable with no explicit time dependence that commutes with the Hamiltonian is a constant of motion. Its mean is constant, and any initially definite value remains definite and unchanged. Quantum numbers labeling conserved observables are called good quantum numbers.
Whether a quantity is conserved depends on the system’s Hamiltonian. An operator always commutes with itself, so energy is always conserved.

title: 5  Time Evolution
text:
5.5 Exercises
5.1. An electron has magnetic moment \({\bf{\mu }} = {{ - 2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}{\bf{S}}} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{ - 2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}{\bf{S}}} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }\) and magnetic energy \(H = - {\bf{\mu }} \cdot {\bf{B}}\). Place a stationary electron in a static field \({\bf{B}} = B{\bf{\hat z}}\).

Given the initial condition \({S_z} = - {\hbar \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {\hbar 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}\), find \(\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle\).
Let \({\bf{\hat n}}\) be a unit vector in the first quadrant of the \(x\)–\(z\) plane, making angle \(\theta\) with \(z\). Initially the projection of \({\bf{S}}\) along \({\bf{\hat n}}\) is \({\hbar \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {\hbar 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}\). Using the preceding chapter’s exercises, find spin state \(\left\vert  {\psi \left( t \right)} \right\rangle\) at time \(t\) and the expectation value of \({\hat S_x},\;{\hat S_y},\;{\hat S_z}\). You may define \({\omega _L} \equiv {{2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}B} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}B} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }\) to simplify the result.

title: 6  * Transitions
text:
6.1 Magnetic resonance
A state that is not an energy eigenstate evolves and can exhibit oscillations. Here we begin in an eigenstate of a dominant Hamiltonian and apply a small periodic perturbation that does not commute with it. This can drive oscillations between its eigenstates. Electron spin in a magnetic field remains our example.
An electron in static field \({{\bf{B}}_0} = {B_0}{\bf{\hat z}}\) initially has spin state \(\vert U\rangle\). States \(\vert U\rangle\) and \(\vert D\rangle\) have energies \({\mu _{\rm{B}}}B\) and \(- {\mu _{\rm{B}}}{B_0}\). Both are stationary, so the system remains in either state without a perturbation. Apply a transverse oscillating field \({\bf{B'}}\) at frequency \(\omega\), perpendicular to \({{\bf{B}}_0}\), with \(\left\vert  {{\bf{B'}}} \right\vert  \ll \left\vert  {{{\bf{B}}_0}} \right\vert\). Although weak, the periodic perturbation can profoundly affect the evolution under suitable conditions.
Write the transverse field as
\[
{\bf{B'}} = {B'_x}{\bf{\hat x}} + {B'_y}{\bf{\hat y}}
\tag{6.1}\]
Let \({\bf{B'}}\) be a constant-magnitude circularly polarized field rotating in the same sense as the electron’s precession in \({{\bf{B}}_0}\):
\[
{B'_x} = B'\cos \omega t; \qquad  \qquad  {B'_y} = B'\sin \omega t
\tag{6.2}\]
The interaction Hamiltonian for the total field is
\[
\hat H = - {{\bf{\mu }}_{\rm{S}}} \cdot \left( {{{\bf{B}}_0} + {\bf{B'}}} \right) = {\hat H_0} + \hat V(t)
\tag{6.3}\]
Here \({\hat H_0}\) and \(\hat V\) are the static-field and oscillating-field energy operators. In the \({\hat \sigma _z}\) representation,
\[
{\hat H_0} = - {{\bf{\mu }}_{\rm{S}}} \cdot {{\bf{B}}_0} = {\mu _{\rm{B}}}{\hat \sigma _z}{B_0} \buildrel\textstyle.\over= {\mu _{\rm{B}}}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{B_0}}&0\\ 0&{ - {B_0}} \end{array}} \right) = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\omega _0}}&0\\ 0&{ - {\omega _0}} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.4}\]
Here \({\omega _0} \equiv {{({E_1} - {E_2})} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{({E_1} - {E_2})} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar } = {{2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}{B_0}} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}{B_0}} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }\) is the static-field Larmor frequency.
\[
\begin{array}{c} \hat V(t) = - {{\bf{\mu }}_{\rm{S}}} \cdot {\bf{B'}} = {\mu _{\rm{B}}}\left( {{{\hat \sigma }_x}{{B'}_x} + {{\hat \sigma }_y}{{B'}_y}} \right) \buildrel\textstyle.\over= {\mu _{\rm{B}}}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{{{B'}_x} - i{{B'}_y}}\\ {{{B'}_x} + i{{B'}_y}}&0 \end{array}} \right)\\ = {\mu _{\rm{B}}}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{B'{e^{ - i\omega t}}}\\ {B'{e^{i\omega t}}}&0 \end{array}} \right) = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{{\Omega _0}{e^{ - i\omega t}}}\\ {{\Omega _0}{e^{i\omega t}}}&0 \end{array}} \right) \end{array}
\tag{6.5}\]
The quantity \({\Omega _0} \equiv {{2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}B'} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}B'} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }\) is the Rabi frequency, or resonant Rabi frequency. Rabi received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Physics for the atomic and molecular beam magnetic-resonance method.
The total Hamiltonian is therefore
\[
\hat H \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\omega _0}}&{{\Omega _0}{e^{ - i\omega t}}}\\ {{\Omega _0}{e^{i\omega t}}}&{ - {\omega _0}} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.6}\]
Expand spin state \(\vert {\psi (t)}\rangle\) at time \(t\) in the \({\hat \sigma _z}\) representation, incorporating the initial condition:
\[
\vert {\psi (t)}\rangle = {c_1}(t)\vert U\rangle + {c_2}(t)\left\vert  D \right\rangle \buildrel\textstyle.\over= \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{c_1}(t)}\\ {{c_2}(t)} \end{array}} \right), \qquad  {\left\vert  {{c_1}} \right\vert ^2} + {\left\vert  {{c_2}} \right\vert ^2} = 1,\;\;\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{c_1}(0) = 1}\\ {{c_2}(0) = 0} \end{array}} \right),\;\;
\tag{6.7}\]
Substituting Equation 6.6 and Equation 6.7 into the Schrödinger equation gives
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{{\dot c}_1}}\\ {{{\dot c}_2}} \end{array}} \right) = - \frac{i}{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\omega _0}}&{{\Omega _0}{e^{ - i\omega t}}}\\ {{\Omega _0}{e^{i\omega t}}}&{ - {\omega _0}} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{c_1}}\\ {{c_2}} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.8}\]
Introduce a rotating-frame transformation:1
\[
{c_1}(t) = {d_1}(t){e^{ - {{i\omega t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i\omega t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}}; \qquad  {c_2}(t) = {d_2}(t){e^{{{i\omega t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i\omega t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}}.
\tag{6.9}\]
Equation Equation 6.8 becomes a system without the rapid oscillating factors:
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{{\dot d}_1}}\\ {{{\dot d}_2}} \end{array}} \right) = \frac{i}{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} \Delta &{ - {\Omega _0}}\\ { - {\Omega _0}}&{ - \Delta } \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{d_1}}\\ {{d_2}} \end{array}} \right), \qquad  \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{d_1}(0)}\\ {{d_2}(0)} \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1\\ 0 \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.10}\]
Here \(\Delta \equiv \omega - {\omega _0}\) is the detuning. The solution of Equation 6.10 is given below; the derivation appears in this chapter’s appendix.
\[
\begin{array}{l} {d_1}(t) = \cos \frac{{\Omega t}}{2} + i\frac{\Delta }{\Omega }\sin \frac{{\Omega t}}{2}\\ {d_2}(t) = - i\frac{{{\Omega _0}}}{\Omega }\sin \frac{{\Omega t}}{2} \end{array}
\tag{6.11}\]
The quantity \(\Omega \equiv \sqrt {{\Delta ^2} + \Omega _0^2}\) is the generalized Rabi frequency. Substituting Equation 6.11 into Equation 6.9 and then Equation 6.7 gives \(\vert {\psi (t)}\rangle\) at any time. The probabilities of states \(\vert U\rangle\) and \(\vert D\rangle\) are
\[
\begin{gathered} {P_1}(t) \equiv {\left\vert  {{c_1}(t)} \right\vert ^2} = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \frac{{{\Delta ^2}}}{{{\Omega ^2}}}} \right) + \frac{1}{2}\frac{{\Omega _0^2}}{{{\Omega ^2}}}\cos \Omega t\xrightarrow{{\Delta = 0}}\frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \cos {\Omega _0}t} \right)  \\ {P_2}(t) \equiv {\left\vert  {{c_2}(t)} \right\vert ^2} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{{\Omega _0^2}}{{{\Omega ^2}}}\left( {1 - \cos \Omega t} \right)\xrightarrow{{\Delta = 0}}\frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - \cos {\Omega _0}t} \right)  \\ \Delta \equiv \omega - {\omega _0},\, \qquad  {\Omega _0} \equiv {{2{\mu _{\text{B}}}B'} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{2{\mu _{\text{B}}}B'} \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }, \qquad  \;\;\;\;\;\;\Omega \equiv \sqrt {{\Delta ^2} + \Omega _0^2} ,  \\ \end{gathered}
\tag{6.12}\]
Both \({P}_{1}\) and \({P}_{2}\) oscillate at \(\Omega\), describing population transfer between the two levels.
Figure 6.1 plots \({P_2}\) for several detunings. At \(\Delta = 0\), \({P_2}\) oscillates most slowly but with maximum contrast, ranging from zero to one. The condition \(\Delta = 0\) is resonance. Increasing detuning increases the oscillation frequency of \({P_2}\) but reduces its amplitude and the transition probability. By Equation 6.12, whenever \(\Omega t\) is an even multiple of \(\pi\), \({P}_{2}=0\) and \({P}_{1}=1\), so the initial population returns. Whenever \(\Omega t\) is an odd multiple of \(\pi\), \({P}_{2}\) reaches its maximum for that detuning. At resonance, \({P}_{2}=1\), corresponding to complete transfer to the other level.
The drive \({\bf{B'}}\) makes \({P}_{2}\) oscillate at \(\Omega\). As \({P}_{2}\) increases, the electron’s mean magnetic energy decreases, transferring energy to the drive: stimulated emission. As \({P}_{2}\) decreases, its mean energy increases by absorbing energy from the drive: stimulated absorption. Both arise from the same mechanism, explaining the equality of Einstein’s corresponding coefficients for this two-state case.
By Equation 6.12, the oscillatory amplitudes of \({P}_{2}\) and \({P}_{1}\) are both
\[
{P_0}(\Delta ) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{{\Omega _0^2}}{{{\Omega ^2}}} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{{\Omega _0^2}}{{{\Delta ^2} + \Omega _0^2}}
\tag{6.13}\]
At fixed \({\Omega _0}\), \({P_0}(\Delta )\) is a peaked function of detuning \(\Delta\), as in Figure 6.2. Its half-width at half-maximum (HWHM) is \({\Omega _0}\). Since \({\Omega _0}\) is proportional to drive amplitude, stronger excitation broadens the line. This power broadening occurs in magnetic-resonance and spectroscopic measurements of level separations, such as absorption spectra.
We can also calculate the evolution of the mean spin vector \(\langle {\psi (t)}\vert {{{\hat S}_{x,y,z}}}\vert {\psi (t)}\rangle\).
\[
\begin{gathered} \langle {{{\hat S}_z}}(t)\rangle = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {c_1^*,}&{c_2^*} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1&0 \\ 0&{ - 1} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{c_1}} \\ {{c_2}} \end{array}} \right) = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {{{\left\vert  {{c_1}} \right\vert }^2} - {{\left\vert  {{c_2}} \right\vert }^2}} \right) \\ = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left[ {\left( {1 - \frac{{\Omega _0^2}}{{{\Omega ^2}}}} \right) + \frac{{\Omega _0^2}}{{{\Omega ^2}}}\cos \Omega t} \right]\xrightarrow{{\Delta = 0}}\frac{\hbar }{2}\cos {\Omega _0}t \\ \end{gathered}
\tag{6.14}\]
\[
\begin{gathered} \langle {{{\hat S}_x}(t)}\rangle = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {c_1^*,}&{c_2^*} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&1 \\ 1&0 \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{c_1}} \\ {{c_2}} \end{array}} \right) = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {{c_1}c_2^* + c_1^*{c_2}} \right) \\ = \frac{\hbar }{2}\frac{{{\Omega _0}}}{{{\Omega ^2}}}\left[ {\Omega \sin \Omega t\sin \omega t - \Delta (1 - \cos \Omega t)\cos \omega t} \right] \\ \xrightarrow{{\Delta = 0}}\frac{\hbar }{2}\sin {\Omega _0}t\sin {\omega _0}t \\ \end{gathered}
\tag{6.15}\]
\[
\begin{gathered} \langle {{{\hat S}_y}(t)}\rangle = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {c_1^*,}&{c_2^*} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{ - i} \\ i&0 \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{c_1}} \\ {{c_2}} \end{array}} \right) = \frac{{i\hbar }}{2}\left( {{c_1}c_2^* - c_1^*{c_2}} \right) \\ = - \frac{\hbar }{2}\frac{{{\Omega _0}}}{{{\Omega ^2}}}\left[ {\Omega \sin \Omega t\cos \omega t + \Delta (1 - \cos \Omega t)\sin \omega t} \right] \\ \xrightarrow{{\Delta = 0}} - \frac{\hbar }{2}\sin {\Omega _0}t\cos {\omega _0}t \\ \end{gathered}
\tag{6.16}\]
A linearly polarized drive \({\bf{B'}}\) is easier to produce than a circularly polarized one. For polarization along \(x\) with amplitude \(2B'\), write \({\bf{B'}}\) as
\[
{B'_x} = 2B'\cos \omega t; \qquad  \qquad  {B'_y} = 0
\tag{6.17}\]
Its interaction \({\bf{B'}}\) with the electron magnetic moment has Hamiltonian
\[
\begin{array}{c} \hat V(t) = 2{\mu _{\rm{B}}}B'\cos \omega t\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&1\\ 1&0 \end{array}} \right) = \hbar \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{{\Omega _0}\cos \omega t}\\ {{\Omega _0}\cos \omega t}&0 \end{array}} \right)\\ = \frac{\hbar }{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{{\Omega _0}({e^{i\omega t}} + {e^{ - i\omega t}})}\\ {{\Omega _0}({e^{i\omega t}} + {e^{ - i\omega t}})}&0 \end{array}} \right) \end{array}
\tag{6.18}\]
Following Equation 6.5 through Equation 6.8, the Schrödinger equation becomes
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{{\dot c}_1}}\\ {{{\dot c}_2}} \end{array}} \right) = - \frac{i}{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\omega _0}}&{{\Omega _0}({e^{i\omega t}} + {e^{ - i\omega t}})}\\ {{\Omega _0}({e^{i\omega t}} + {e^{ - i\omega t}})}&{ - {\omega _0}} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{c_1}}\\ {{c_2}} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.19}\]
Using the definitions and method following Equation 6.9 gives
\[
\begin{array}{c} {{\dot d}_1} = \frac{i}{2}\left[ {\Delta {d_1} - {\Omega _0}({e^{2i\omega t}} + 1){d_2}} \right],\\ {{\dot d}_2} = \frac{i}{2}\left[ { - {\Omega _0}(1 + {e^{ - 2i\omega t}}){d_1} - \Delta {d_2}} \right], \end{array}
\tag{6.20}\]
Assume \(B' \ll {B_0}\) and near resonance between \(\omega\) and \({\omega _0}\), namely \({\Omega _0},\;\left\vert  \Delta \right\vert  \ll {\omega _0},\omega\). These are the near-resonant, weak-drive conditions. In Equation 6.20, the factors \({e^{ \pm 2i\omega t}}\) oscillate much faster than changes on the scales \(\Delta\) and \({\Omega _0}\), so they may be replaced by their zero time average. This is the rotating-wave approximation. Equation Equation 6.20 then reduces to Equation 6.10 and has the same solution. A weak near-resonant linear drive is therefore approximately equivalent to a circular drive with half its amplitude.

title: 6  * Transitions
section: 6.2 Transitions in a general two-level system
text:
6.2 Transitions in a general two-level system
The magnetic-resonance analysis extends to other two-level transitions. For any two-level system of separation \(\hbar {\omega _0}\), shifting the energy origin gives the unperturbed eigenvalue equation
\[
\begin{array}{l} {{\hat H}_0}\vert e\rangle = \hbar \frac{{{\omega _0}}}{2}\vert e\rangle \\ {{\hat H}_0}\vert g\rangle = - \hbar \frac{{{\omega _0}}}{2}\vert g\rangle \end{array}
\tag{6.21}\]
Here \(\vert e\rangle ,{\rm{ }}\vert g\rangle\) denote excited and ground states. In the \({\hat H_0}\) representation,
\[
{\hat H_0} = \hbar \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{{{\omega _0}} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{{\omega _0}} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}&0\\ 0&{{{ - {\omega _0}} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{ - {\omega _0}} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.22}\]
Adding a perturbation \(\hat V(t) = {\hat V_0}\cos \omega t\) gives
\[
\hat V(t) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\langle 1\vert {{{\hat V}_0}}\vert 1\rangle }&{\langle 1\vert {{{\hat V}_0}}\vert 2\rangle }\\ {{{\langle 1\vert {{{\hat V}}_0}\vert 2\rangle }^*}}&{\langle 2\vert {{{\hat V}_0}}\vert 2\rangle } \end{array}} \right)\cos \omega t
\tag{6.23}\]
Frequently \({\hat V_0}\) has zero diagonal elements, \(\langle 1\vert {{{\hat V}_0}}\vert 1\rangle = \langle 2\vert {{{\hat V}_0}}\vert 2\rangle = 0\), and \(\langle 1\vert {{{\hat V}_0}}\vert 2\rangle\) is real. Defining \({\Omega _0} \equiv {{\langle 1\vert {{{\hat V}_0}}\vert 2\rangle } \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{\langle 1\vert {{{\hat V}_0}}\vert 2\rangle } \hbar }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } \hbar }\) gives
\[
\hat V(t) = \hbar \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 0&{{\Omega _0}\cos \omega t}\\ {\Omega _0^{}\cos \omega t}&0 \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.24}\]
Equations Equation 6.22 and Equation 6.24 have the same form as Equation 6.4 and Equation 6.18. Such a two-level transition is therefore mathematically equivalent to spin-1/2 magnetic resonance.

title: 6  * Transitions
section: 6.3 * Density matrices and the Bloch vector
text:
6.3 * Density matrices and the Bloch vector
The preceding sections reduce two-level evolution to Equation 6.11, the evolution of \({d_1},{d_2}\). We now give it a geometric interpretation.
An arbitrary pure state of a two-level system can be written as
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{d_1}}\\ {{d_2}} \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\cos \frac{\theta }{2}}\\ {{e^{i\phi }}\sin \frac{\theta }{2}} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.25}\]
Define the Cartesian Bloch vector \({\bf{P}} = \left\{ {u,v,w} \right\}\):
\[
\begin{array}{l} u = {\rho _{12}} + {\rho _{21}}\\ v = i({\rho _{12}} - {\rho _{21}})\\ \omega = {\rho _{11}} - {\rho _{22}} \end{array}
\tag{6.26}\]
where
\[
{\rho _{ij}} \equiv {d_i}d_j^*
\tag{6.27}\]
\[
\begin{array}{l} {\rho _{12}} = \frac{1}{2}{e^{ - i\phi }}\sin \theta \\ {\rho _{21}} = \frac{1}{2}{e^{i\phi }}\sin \theta \\ {\rho _{11}} = \frac{{1 + \cos \theta }}{2}\\ {\rho _{22}} = \frac{{1 - \cos \theta }}{2} \end{array}
\tag{6.28}\]
By Equation 6.26,
\[
\begin{array}{l} u = {\rho _{12}} + {\rho _{21}} = \sin \theta \cos \phi \\ v = i({\rho _{12}} - {\rho _{21}}) = \sin \theta \sin \phi \\ \omega = {\rho _{11}} - {\rho _{22}} = \cos \theta \end{array}
\tag{6.29}\]
One verifies \({u^2} + {v^2} + {w^2} = 1\), so \({\bf{P}}\) is a unit vector. The parameters \(\theta ,\phi\) are its spherical angles. All pure states lie on the surface traced by its tip, the Bloch sphere. For example,
\[
\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\left( {0,0,1} \right) \leftrightarrow \;\vert U\rangle }&{\left( {0,0, - 1} \right) \leftrightarrow \;\vert D\rangle }\\ {\left( {1,0,0} \right) \leftrightarrow \;\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\;\vert U\rangle + \;\vert D\rangle } \right)}&{\left( { - 1,0,0} \right) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\;\vert U\rangle - \;\vert D\rangle } \right)}\\ {\left( {0,1,0} \right) \leftrightarrow \;\;\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\;\vert U\rangle + i\;\vert D\rangle } \right)}&{\left( {0, - 1,0} \right) \leftrightarrow \;\frac{1}{{\sqrt 2 }}\left( {\;\vert U\rangle - i\;\vert D\rangle } \right)} \end{array}
\tag{6.30}\]
The motion of \({\bf{P}}\) describes state evolution Equation 6.10. From Equation 6.10 and Equation 6.27,
\[
\begin{array}{l} {{\dot \rho }_{12}} = i\Delta {\rho _{12}} + i\frac{{{\Omega _0}}}{2}\left( {{\rho _{11}} - {\rho _{22}}} \right)\\ {{\dot \rho }_{21}} = - i\Delta {\rho _{21}} - i\frac{{{\Omega _0}}}{2}\left( {{\rho _{11}} - {\rho _{22}}} \right)\\ {{\dot \rho }_{11}} = i\frac{{{\Omega _0}}}{2}\left( {{\rho _{12}} - {\rho _{21}}} \right)\\ {{\dot \rho }_{22}} = - i\frac{{{\Omega _0}}}{2}\left( {{\rho _{12}} - {\rho _{21}}} \right) \end{array}
\tag{6.31}\]
Using Equation 6.31 and Equation 6.26,
\[
\begin{array}{l} \frac{{du}}{{dt}} = \Delta v\\ \frac{{dv}}{{dt}} = - \Delta u - {\Omega _0}w\\ \frac{{dw}}{{dt}} = {\Omega _0}v \end{array}
\tag{6.32}\]
Define \({\bf{\Omega }} = \left\{ {{\Omega _0},0, - \Delta } \right\}\). Equation Equation 6.32 becomes
\[
\frac{{d{\bf{P}}}}{{dt}} = {\bf{\Omega }} \times {\bf{P}}
\tag{6.33}\]
Since \({\bf{\Omega }}\) is constant, Equation 6.33 describes \({\bf{P}}\) precessing about \({\bf{\Omega }}\) with angular speed \(\left\vert  {\bf{\Omega }} \right\vert  = \sqrt {\Omega _0^2 + {\Delta ^2}}\). Under the preceding rotating-wave treatment, two-state dynamics thus becomes a Bloch-vector equation,2 giving a useful geometric picture of transitions.
This corresponds to the group-theoretic connection between a unitary transformation \({\rm{SU}}(2)\) in a two-dimensional complex space and a rotation \({\rm{SO}}(3)\) in three-dimensional Cartesian space.

title: 6  * Transitions
text:
6.4 Appendix
We solve the linear differential system Equation 6.10 as follows.
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{{\dot d}_1}}\\ {{{\dot d}_2}} \end{array}} \right) = \frac{i}{2}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} \Delta &{ - {\Omega _0}}\\ { - {\Omega _0}}&{ - \Delta } \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{d_1}}\\ {{d_2}} \end{array}} \right), \qquad  \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{d_1}(0)}\\ {{d_2}(0)} \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1\\ 0 \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.34}\]
Try \(\left( {{d_1},{d_2}} \right) = \left( {{k_1},{k_2}} \right){e^{{{i\lambda t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i\lambda t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}}\), with time-independent \({k_{1,2}}\). Substitution gives the eigenvalue equation
\[
\lambda \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{k_1}}\\ {{k_2}} \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} \Delta &{ - {\Omega _0}}\\ { - {\Omega _0}}&{ - \Delta } \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{k_1}}\\ {{k_2}} \end{array}} \right) \Rightarrow \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\Delta - \lambda }&{ - {\Omega _0}}\\ { - {\Omega _0}}&{ - \Delta - \lambda } \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{k_1}}\\ {{k_2}} \end{array}} \right) = 0,
\tag{6.35}\]
A nonzero solution requires
\[
\left\vert  {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\Delta - \lambda }&{ - {\Omega _0}}\\ { - {\Omega _0}}&{ - \Delta - \lambda } \end{array}} \right\vert  = 0
\tag{6.36}\]
The eigenvalues are \({\lambda _ \pm } = \pm \Omega\), where \(\Omega \equiv \sqrt {\Omega _0^2 + {\Delta ^2}}\). Substituting \({\lambda _ \pm }\) into Equation 6.35 gives the eigenvectors
\[
\vert \lambda\rangle \equiv \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{k_1}}\\ {{k_2}} \end{array}} \right): \qquad  \vert {{\lambda _ + }}\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\Omega _0}}\\ {\Delta - \Omega } \end{array}} \right), \qquad  \vert {{\lambda _ - }}\rangle = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\Omega _0}}\\ {\Delta + \Omega } \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.37}\]
The general solution is a linear combination of these particular solutions:
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{d_1}(t)}\\ {{d_2}(t)} \end{array}} \right) = {g_ + }\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\Omega _0}}\\ {\Delta - \Omega } \end{array}} \right)\exp \left( {{{i{\lambda _ + }t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{\lambda _ + }t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}} \right) + {g_ - }\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\Omega _0}}\\ {\Delta + \Omega } \end{array}} \right)\exp \left( {{{i{\lambda _ - }t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{\lambda _ - }t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}} \right)
\tag{6.38}\]
Determine coefficients \({g_ \pm }\) from the initial condition:
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1\\ 0 \end{array}} \right) = {g_ + }\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\Omega _0}}\\ {\Delta - \Omega } \end{array}} \right) + {g_ - }\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\Omega _0}}\\ {\Delta + \Omega } \end{array}} \right) = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{\Omega _0}}&{{\Omega _0}}\\ {\Delta - \Omega }&{\Delta + \Omega } \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{g_ + }}\\ {{g_ - }} \end{array}} \right) = D\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{g_ + }}\\ {{g_ - }} \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.39}\]
Therefore,
\[
\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{g_ + }}\\ {{g_ - }} \end{array}} \right) = {D^{ - 1}}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1\\ 0 \end{array}} \right) = \frac{1}{{2{\Omega _0}\Omega }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\Omega + \Delta }&{ - {\Omega _0}}\\ {\Omega - \Delta }&{{\Omega _0}} \end{array}} \right)\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} 1\\ 0 \end{array}} \right) = \frac{1}{{2{\Omega _0}\Omega }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\Omega + \Delta }\\ {\Omega - \Delta } \end{array}} \right)
\tag{6.40}\]
Substituting \({g_ \pm }\) into Equation 6.38 gives
\[
\begin{array}{c} \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {{d_1}(t)}\\ {{d_2}(t)} \end{array}} \right) = \frac{1}{{2{\Omega _0}\Omega }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {(\Omega + \Delta ){\Omega _0}}\\ {(\Omega + \Delta )(\Delta - \Omega )} \end{array}} \right){e^{{{i{\lambda _ + }t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{\lambda _ + }t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}} + \frac{1}{{2{\Omega _0}\Omega }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {(\Omega - \Delta ){\Omega _0}}\\ {(\Omega - \Delta )(\Delta + \Omega )} \end{array}} \right){e^{{{i{\lambda _ - }t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{\lambda _ - }t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}}\\ = \frac{1}{{2{\Omega _0}\Omega }}\left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {(\Omega + \Delta ){\Omega _0}{e^{{{i\Omega t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i\Omega t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}} + (\Omega - \Delta ){\Omega _0}{e^{{{ - i\Omega t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{ - i\Omega t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}}}\\ { - \Omega _0^2{e^{{{i\Omega t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i\Omega t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}} + \Omega _0^2{e^{{{ - i\Omega t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{ - i\Omega t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}}}} \end{array}} \right)\\ = = \left( {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\cos \left( {\frac{\Omega }{2}t} \right) + \frac{{i\Delta }}{\Omega }\sin \left( {\frac{\Omega }{2}t} \right)}\\ { - \frac{{i{\Omega _0}}}{\Omega }\sin \left( {\frac{\Omega }{2}t} \right)} \end{array}} \right) \end{array}
\tag{6.41}\]

title: 6  * Transitions
text:
Some books use the interaction picture, setting \({c_1}(t) = {d_1}(t)\exp ( - {{i{\omega _0}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{\omega _0}t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2}); \qquad  {c_2}(t) = {d_2}(t)\exp ({{i{\omega _0}t} \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {{i{\omega _0}t} 2}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } 2})\). The method used here is equivalent to a rotating coordinate frame in classical mechanics and gives a shorter derivation for a two-level system.↩︎
Feynman, Vernon, and Hellwarth, “GEOMETRICAL REPRESENTATION OF THE SCHRODINGER EQUATION FOR SOLVING MASER PROBLEMS.”↩︎

title: 7  Continuous Observables
text:
7.1 The Dirac delta function
So far, our observables have discrete eigenvalues. Their eigenbases define discrete representations. We now consider observables with continuous eigenvalues and the continuous representations they define, developing their properties by comparison. Unless stated otherwise, integrals extend from negative to positive infinity.
Introduce the Dirac \(\delta\) function \(\delta (x - x')\), where \(x\) is a real variable and \(x'\) a real parameter. It is defined by
\[
\delta \left( {x - x'} \right) = \left\{ {\begin{array}{*{20}{c}} {\infty ,}&{x = x'}\\ {0,}&{x \ne x'} \end{array}} \right.
\tag{7.1}\]
\[
\int_{ - \infty }^\infty {\delta \left( {x - x'} \right)dx} = 1
\tag{7.2}\]
The \(\delta\) function has the properties
\[
\delta \left( {x - x'} \right) = \delta \left( {x' - x} \right)
\tag{7.3}\]
\[
\delta \left( {x - x'} \right)F\left( x \right) = \delta \left( {x - x'} \right)F\left( {x'} \right)
\tag{7.4}\]
\[
\int {dx\;\delta \left( {x - x'} \right)F\left( x \right)} = F\left( {x'} \right)
\tag{7.5}\]
Equation Equation 7.5 may itself be used to define the \(\delta\) function.
A Fourier expansion expresses a function \(F\left( x \right)\) in terms of \(\exp \left( {ikx} \right)\):
\[
F\left( x \right) = \frac{1}{{\sqrt {2\pi } }}\int\limits_{{\rm{ - }}\infty }^{{\rm{ + }}\infty } {dk\;\widetilde F\left( k \right)\exp \left( {ikx} \right)}
\tag{7.6}\]
The coefficients \(\widetilde F\left( k \right)\) are
\[
\widetilde F\left( k \right) = \frac{1}{{\sqrt {2\pi } }}\int\limits_{{\rm{ - }}\infty }^\infty {dx\;F\left( x \right)\exp \left( { - ikx} \right)}
\tag{7.7}\]
Functions \(F\left( x \right)\) and \(\widetilde F\left( k \right)\) are Fourier transforms of each other. Equations Equation 7.6 and Equation 7.7 give
\[
\begin{array}{c} F\left( {x'} \right) = \frac{1}{{\sqrt {2\pi } }}\int {dk\;\widetilde F\left( k \right)\exp \left( {ikx'} \right)} \\ = \frac{1}{{\sqrt {2\pi } }}\int {dk\;\left[ {\frac{1}{{\sqrt {2\pi } }}\int\limits_{{\rm{ - }}\infty }^\infty {dx\;F\left( x \right)\exp \left( { - ikx} \right)} } \right]\exp \left( {ikx'} \right)} \\ = \int {dx\left\{ {\frac{1}{{2\pi }}\int {dk\exp \left[ {ik\left( {x' - x} \right)} \right]} } \right\}F\left( x \right)} \\ = \int {dx\left\{ {\frac{1}{{2\pi }}\int {dk\exp \left[ {ik\left( {x - x'} \right)} \right]} } \right\}F\left( x \right)} \end{array}
\tag{7.8}\]
Comparing Equation 7.8 with the defining identity Equation 7.5 gives
\[
\delta \left( {x - x'} \right) = \frac{1}{{2\pi }}\int_{ - \infty }^\infty {dk\exp \left[ {ik\left( {x - x'} \right)} \right]}
\tag{7.9}\]
\[
\delta \left( x \right) = \frac{1}{{2\pi }}\int_{ - \infty }^\infty {dk\exp \left( {ikx} \right)} = \frac{1}{{\sqrt {2\pi } }}\int_{ - \infty }^\infty {dk\frac{1}{{\sqrt {2\pi } }}\exp \left( {ikx} \right)}
\tag{7.10}\]
This is the Fourier representation of the \(\delta\) function. Comparing Equation 7.10 and Equation 7.6, \(\delta (x)\) and \({1 \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {1 {\sqrt {2\pi } }}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\sqrt {2\pi } }}\) form a Fourier-transform pair.

title: 7  Continuous Observables
text:
7.2 Continuous representations and wavefunctions
We extend the discrete formalism to continuous observables. For discrete eigenvalues of \(\hat Q\), use integer-indexed quantities \({q_i}\). For continuous eigenvalues of \(\hat Q\), use a continuous variable \(q,q',q''...\).


Figure 7.1. Left: \({\left\vert  {\langle {{q_i}}\vert \psi\rangle } \right\vert ^2}\) is a probability in a discrete representation. Right: \({\left\vert  {\langle q\vert \psi\rangle } \right\vert ^2}\) is a probability density in a continuous representation.

For a discrete observable \(\hat Q\), state \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) has the expansion in the \(\hat Q\) representation
\[
\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \sum\limits_i {\left\vert  {{q_i}} \right\rangle \left\langle {{{q_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{q_i}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle }
\tag{7.11}\]
The probability amplitude \(\langle {{q_i}}\vert \psi\rangle\) is a discrete function of \({q_i}\). Its squared magnitude \({\left\vert  {\left\langle {{{q_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{q_i}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2}\) is the probability that \(\hat Q\) has value \({q}_{i}\) in state \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\). Probability conservation requires
\[
\sum\limits_i {{{\left\vert  {\left\langle {{{q_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{q_i}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } \right\vert }^2}} = 1
\tag{7.12}\]
For a continuous observable \(\hat Q\), \(\left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle\) becomes a continuous function of \(q\), written
\[
\left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle \equiv \psi \left( q \right)
\tag{7.13}\]
This is a wavefunction, although it need not describe an ordinary wave. It depends on the representation: \(\psi \left( q \right)\) is state \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) in the \(\hat Q\) representation. As Figure 7.1 illustrates, \({\left\vert  {\psi (q)} \right\vert ^2}\) is continuous in \(q\), so the sum in Equation 7.12 becomes an integral:
\[
\int {dq} {\left\vert  {\psi (q)} \right\vert ^2} = 1
\tag{7.14}\]
Thus \(dq{\left\vert  {\psi (q)} \right\vert ^2}\) is the probability that \(\hat Q\) lies in \(q\~q + dq\) in state \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\). The quantity \({\left\vert  {\psi (q)} \right\vert ^2}\) is the probability density near \(q\) for \(\hat Q\) in state \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\), with dimensions \({1 \mathord{\left/ {\vphantom {1 q}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } q}\).
To ensure unique, normalized probabilities, the physically admissible wavefunctions \(\psi (q)\) considered here satisfy three conditions:

Single-valued: apart from an overall phase, each \(q\) has a unique value \(\psi (q)\).
Continuous everywhere.
Vanishing at infinity: \(\psi (q = \pm \infty ) = 0\).

Normalization and probability conservation Equation 7.14 give, for any state \(\vert \psi \rangle\),
\[
\left\langle {\psi } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\psi \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle = 1 = \int {dq} {\left\vert  {\left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } \right\vert ^2} = \int {dq\left\langle {\psi } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\psi q}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {q} \right\rangle \left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } = \left\langle \psi \right\vert \left( {\int {dq\left\vert  q \right\rangle \left\langle q \right\vert } } \right)\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle
\tag{7.15}\]
Hence the continuous completeness relation is
\[
\int {dq\;\left\vert  q \right\rangle \left\langle q \right\vert } = \hat I
\tag{7.16}\]
Completeness gives the following results.
The expansion of an arbitrary state \(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle\) is
\[
\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \int {dq\left\vert  q \right\rangle \left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } = \int {dq\;\psi (q)\left\vert  q \right\rangle }
\tag{7.17}\]
The inner product of two states is
\[
\left\langle {\phi } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\phi \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle = \int {dq\left\langle {\phi } \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {\phi q}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {q} \right\rangle \left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } = \int {{\phi ^*}\left( q \right)\psi \left( q \right)dq}
\tag{7.18}\]
Take the inner product of Equation 7.17 with eigenstate \(\vert {q'}\rangle\) of \(\hat Q\), belonging to eigenvalue \(q'\):
\[
\psi (q') = \int {dq\;\psi (q)\left\langle {{q'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{q'} q}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {q} \right\rangle }
\tag{7.19}\]
Comparison with the \(\delta\)-function definition Equation 7.5 gives
\[
\left\langle {{q'}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{q'} q}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {q} \right\rangle = \delta (q - q') = \delta (q' - q) = \left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q {q'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{q'}} \right\rangle
\tag{7.20}\]
Thus the state with definite value \(q'\) of continuous observable \(\hat Q\) has wavefunction \(\delta (q - q')\) in its own representation.
Table 7.1 compares the corresponding formulas in discrete and continuous representations.

\(\left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q {q'}}} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {{q'}} \right\rangle = \delta \left( {q - q'} \right)\)

\(\left\vert  \psi \right\rangle = \int {dq\left\vert  q \right\rangle \left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } = \int {dq\;\psi (q)\left\vert  q \right\rangle }\)

\(\sum\limits_i {{{\left\vert  {\left\langle {{{q_i}}} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {{{q_i}} \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } \right\vert }^2}} = 1\)
\(\int {dq\;{{\left\vert  {\left\langle {q} \mathrel{\left \vert  {\vphantom {q \psi }} \right. \kern-1.2pt } {\psi } \right\rangle } \right\vert }^2}} = \int {dq\;{{\left\vert  {\psi (q)} \right\vert }^2}} = 1\)
